  • Velocity saturation (your Chapter 6): at high lateral field carriers reach vsat, so ID ∝ Vov (linear) instead of Vov².
  • Drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL) and punch-through: a high drain voltage reduces the barrier near the source in very short channels.
  • Subthreshold leakage: below Vth the current does not drop to zero but falls exponentially, about 60–100 mV per decade.
  • Gate-oxide leakage: as tox shrinks below 2 nm, electrons tunnel through, motivating high-k dielectrics.
Exam traps for the MOSFET
  • nMOS turns on with a high gate; pMOS turns on with a low gate. Never mix.
  • Threshold voltage is where inversion begins; the channel doesn't appear at any VGS below it.
  • The linear formula holds only while VDS < VGS − Vth.
  • μn is not a constant; in the channel it is lower than in bulk silicon because of surface scattering, and it falls at high gate voltage.
  • "Depletion-mode" is not the same as the "depletion region". The mode name refers to a device with a channel present at zero gate bias.

CHAPTER 11The MOSFET in Depth: Regions, Scaling and Short-Channel Effects

Chapter 10 stopped at the linear-region current. Here is everything after it: saturation, every region of operation, the on-resistance, sub-threshold current, scaling, and the five "second-order" effects your class listed.

Your third note-set (Vlsi-MOS29-09, p.6 to p.14) Instructor's Drive: MOSFET_1, MOSFET_2, MOSFET_3

11.1 Two electric fields inside every MOSFET

Your notes (p.11) draw two arrows inside the device:

Ey: the vertical (transverse) field

Made by the gate, pointing down into the substrate. It creates and holds the channel. Ey ∝ VGS/tox.

Ex: the horizontal (longitudinal) field

Made by the drain, pointing along the channel. It pushes the electrons from source to drain. Ex ∝ VDS/L.

For a long-channel device, Ex ≪ Ey. This is the gradual channel approximation (GCA): the channel charge at each point x is set only by the vertical field there, so we can write Q(x) = W Cox(VGS − Vth − V(x)) exactly as you did on p.8. The Drive notes add a second simplification, the charge-sheet approximation: the inversion layer is treated as having zero thickness. Both hold for long channels and break down when L shrinks to about 0.1 μm, which is where the short-channel effects of §11.8 begin.

Explain like I'm 10

The gate is a magnet held above a road: it decides how many cars (electrons) are on the road. The drain is a slope along the road: it decides how fast they roll. As long as the road is long, the slope is gentle and the magnet is in charge. Make the road very short and the slope becomes a cliff: now the drain starts bossing the cars around too, and the simple formulas stop working.

11.2 From the triode formula to saturation

Start from your boxed equation ① (p.8):

ID = μnCox WL [ (VGS − Vth)VDS − VDS²2 ]   ①

Fix VGS and raise VDS. The formula is a downward parabola in VDS. Your notes (p.9) find its peak by setting the slope to zero:

  1. dIDdVDS = μnCox(W/L)[(VGS − Vth) − VDS] = 0
  2. ⇒ VDS,sat = VGS − Vth (the saturation voltage, equal to the overdrive).
  3. Put it back into ①: (VGS − Vth)(VGS − Vth) − (VGS − Vth)²/2 = ½(VGS − Vth)².
Saturation current (your p.9)
ID,max = ID,sat = 12 μnCox WL (VGS − Vth)²
For VDS ≥ VGS − Vth the current stays at this value: constant, independent of VDS.

Why it stays flat (and doesn't follow the parabola back down): at VDS = VGS − Vth the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end is exactly Vth, so the channel just disappears there: pinch-off. Raising VDS further only moves the pinch-off point a tiny bit toward the source; the voltage across the remaining channel stays at VGS − Vth, so the current through it stays the same. Electrons reaching the pinch-off point are swept across the short depletion gap to the drain by its strong field. The falling half of the parabola is not physical.

Effect of VGS (p.9): a bigger VGS gives a bigger overdrive, so both VDS,sat and the plateau rise. Your sketch shows VGS = 2 V and 4 V; with Vth = 1 V the plateaus are in the ratio (3/1)² = 9 : 1, not 2 : 1. Doubling VGS does not double the current; the overdrive is what gets squared.

Explain like I'm 10

A funnel feeding a bottle. Tilting the funnel more (raising VDS) makes water run faster, until the neck of the funnel is the bottleneck. After that, tilting more changes nothing: the neck (the pinch-off point) lets through a fixed amount. To get more water you need a wider neck, and that is what a bigger VGS does.

11.3 All the regions of operation

Your regions-of-operation table (p.9 to p.11), completed
RegionBiasing (nMOS)ChannelDrain currentPhysical meaning
1. Cut-offVGS < VthnoneID = 0 (ideal)MOSFET OFF
2. Sub-thresholdVGS ≲ Vthweak inversionID ∝ exp[(VGS − Vth)/(nVT)]very small (leakage) current
3. Deep triode / linearVGS > Vth, VDS ≪ VGS − Vthstrong inversion, uniform channelID ≈ μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)VDS  ②voltage-variable resistor
4. Non-linear (triode)VGS > Vth, VDS < VGS − Vthstrong inversion, taperingfull formula ①curving (non-linear) resistor
5. SaturationVGS > Vth, VDS ≥ VGS − Vthpinched off at the drain½μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)²ideal current source

Your table writes the same condition "VDS < VGS − Vth" for rows 3 and 4. The difference is how much smaller: row 3 is the part where VDS²/2 is negligible (a rule of thumb is VDS < 0.1 to 0.2 × (VGS − Vth)), so the curve is still a straight line.

pMOS: the same table with every voltage reversed in sign: VGS < Vtp (both negative) to turn on, and saturation when VDS ≤ VGS − Vtp. The easy way is to use magnitudes: ISD = ½μpCox(W/L)(|VGS| − |Vtp|)² for |VDS| ≥ |VGS| − |Vtp|, with current flowing from source to drain (p.6: "for operating pMOS: VGS −ve, VDS −ve").

How to decide the region in an exam
  1. Is VGS > Vth? If no: cut-off (ID ≈ 0, or sub-threshold if asked).
  2. Compute the overdrive Vov = VGS − Vth.
  3. Compare VDS with Vov: smaller ⇒ triode (use ①); equal or bigger ⇒ saturation.
  4. If the question gives a circuit and you don't know VDS yet: assume saturation, compute ID, find VDS, then check VDS ≥ Vov. If the check fails, redo with ①.

11.4 The on-resistance Ron

Your p.10 drops the VDS²/2 term in the deep-triode region and gets equation ②, which is Ohm's law:

On-resistance (your p.10; Drive MOSFET_2)
Ron = VDSID = 1μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth)
Ron ∝ 1/(overdrive) and ∝ L/W. Change VGS and the resistance changes: a voltage-variable resistor.

This is the resistance in the "switch model" of Chapter 12 and in the delay τ = RonC. It is why designers want a high mobility (nMOS is better than pMOS), a thin oxide (big Cox), a short L and a large overdrive.

Worked: μnCox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 5, Vth = 0.5 V. Find Ron for VGS = 1.0 V and for VGS = 1.8 V. What VGS gives 1 kΩ?
  1. k = μnCox(W/L) = 200 × 5 = 1000 μA/V² = 1 mA/V².
  2. VGS = 1.0 V: overdrive 0.5 V ⇒ Ron = 1/(10-3 × 0.5) = 2 kΩ.
  3. VGS = 1.8 V: overdrive 1.3 V ⇒ Ron = 1/(1.3×10-3) = 769 Ω.
  4. For 1 kΩ: overdrive = 1/(k × 1000) = 1 V ⇒ VGS = 1.5 V.

Check of the "small VDS" assumption: this Ron is only valid while VDS stays well below the overdrive (say below 0.1 V here).

11.5 Sub-threshold conduction

Below Vth the channel is in weak inversion: there are few electrons, and they move mainly by diffusion (not drift) from the source, over a potential barrier, to the drain, just like electrons crossing a forward-biased p–n junction. That is why the current is exponential:

Sub-threshold current (your p.9; Drive LTSpice notes)
ID,sub ∝ exp[ VGS − Vthn VT ] · [ 1 − exp(−VDS/VT) ]
n = ideality (slope) factor, 1 to 1.5    VT = kT/q ≈ 26 mV. The second bracket ≈ 1 once VDS > ~100 mV.
Sub-threshold slope S = n VT ln 10 ≈ n × 60 mV/decade (at 300 K)

Where 60 mV comes from: to raise the current 10×, the exponent must grow by ln 10 = 2.303, so ΔVGS = 2.303 × nVT = 2.303 × 26 mV × n ≈ 60n mV. The Drive notes define S exactly this way: "gate voltage needed to change ID by one decade (e.g. 10-2 → 10-3 A)", ideal 60 mV/decade. No MOSFET at room temperature can switch more sharply than this, because it is set by the thermal spread of electron energies.

Explain like I'm 10

A tap that never closes completely. Turning the handle below the "off" mark makes the drip slower and slower, ten times slower for every 60 mV, but it never reaches exactly zero. A chip has billions of these dripping taps, which is why a phone's battery drains slowly even when the screen is off. This drip is a big part of static power.

Worked: a transistor has S = 80 mV/decade and ID = 1 μA at VGS = Vth. What is the leakage at VGS = 0 if Vth = 0.4 V? What Vth would be needed for 1 pA?
  1. Going from Vth down to 0 is 400 mV = 400/80 = 5 decades.
  2. Ioff = 1 μA × 10-5 = 10 pA.
  3. 1 pA is 6 decades below 1 μA ⇒ Vth = 6 × 80 = 480 mV.

This is the core trade-off of low-power design: a lower Vth gives a faster transistor (more overdrive) but exponentially more leakage.

11.6 The hand-calculation model and its five parameters

From the Drive (MOSFET_3): for manual analysis the MOSFET is described by just five numbers.

ParameterMeaningTypical value
k′ = μnCoxprocess transconductance parameter (fixed by the process)100 to 300 μA/V² (nMOS); about 1/2 to 1/3 of that for pMOS
VT (Vth)threshold voltage at VSB = 00.3 to 0.7 V
λchannel-length modulation0.02 to 0.2 V-1
γbody-effect coefficient0.2 to 0.6 V½
VDSATvelocity-saturation limit on VDS,sata few tenths of a volt in short channels

Device transconductance parameter k = k′(W/L). Also from the Drive: the channel is shorter than drawn because the source and drain diffuse sideways under the gate: Leff = Ldrawn − 2LD (LD = lateral diffusion). Use Leff in W/L for accurate work.

Beyond your notes: transconductance gm

In saturation, gm = ∂ID/∂VGS = μnCox(W/L)(VGS − Vth) = √(2k ID) = 2ID/(VGS − Vth). The LTSpice experiment in your Drive (Chapter 15) measures exactly this from the ID–VGS curve. Output resistance in saturation ro = 1/(λID) (§11.8). Intrinsic gain = gmro.

11.7 Device scaling

Moore's law (the Drive quotes doubling every 1.5 to 2 years) is achieved by scaling: shrinking L, W and tox. Halving each dimension fits four times as many transistors in the same area. The question is what to do with the voltages. Your notes (p.12) list two methods:

1. Constant-field scaling

Shrink the voltages by the same factor as the dimensions, so the fields stay the same. Your example: Ex = VDS/L → (VDS/2)/(L/2) and Ey = VGS/tox → (VGS/3)/(tox/3): unchanged. (The Drive: L 1 → 0.5 μm needs VDS 1 → 0.5 V.)

2. Constant-voltage scaling

Shrink the dimensions but keep the supply voltage. Your notes: "generally used"; the Drive: "often preferred". The practical reason: chips must keep talking to other chips at standard voltages (5 V, 3.3 V, 1.8 V), so the supply can't fall freely.

Beyond your notes: what each method does to the device (scale factor S > 1)
QuantityConstant fieldConstant voltage
L, W, tox, junction depth1/S1/S
VDD, Vth1/S1
Substrate doping NASS²
Electric field1S (dangerous)
Cox = εox/toxSS
Gate capacitance C = CoxWL1/S1/S
Drain current ID ∝ Cox(W/L)V²1/SS
Delay τ ∝ CV/I1/S1/S²
Power per transistor P = VI1/S²S
Area per transistor1/S²1/S²
Power density P/area1S³ (the chip overheats)

Constant-voltage scaling is faster but raises the fields by S, which causes velocity saturation, hot carriers, DIBL and oxide breakdown, and raises power density by S³. Real industry did constant-voltage scaling until about the 1990s and then lowered VDD slowly ("general scaling").

Worked: a 1 μm process with VDD = 5 V and tox = 20 nm is scaled to 0.5 μm. Give tox, VDD, current, delay and power per transistor under each method.

S = 2. Both methods: tox = 10 nm, gate capacitance halves, area quarters.

Constant field: VDD = 2.5 V; ID ×½; delay ×½; power ×¼; power density unchanged.

Constant voltage: VDD = 5 V; ID ×2; delay ×¼; power ×2; power density ×8; fields ×2 (now the short-channel effects below bite).

11.8 Second-order and short-channel effects

These are the five effects listed in your notes (p.12 to p.14), in the same order, with the Drive's explanations added.

1. Body effect

The substrate (body, B) is the fourth terminal. Your notes: nMOS body → most negative potential; pMOS body → most positive potential. Reason (Drive): the source–body and drain–body p–n junctions must stay reverse-biased; if the nMOS body went positive they would forward-bias, a large current would flow and the device could burn out.

If the source sits above the body (VSB > 0, e.g. the upper transistor in a series stack), the source–body junction is more reverse-biased, the depletion region under the channel is thicker and holds more negative charge, so the gate must work harder to invert the surface: Vth rises.

Body effect
Vth = Vth0 + γ ( √(2φF + VSB) − √(2φF) )    γ = √(2qεsNA)Cox
Worked: Vth0 = 0.5 V, γ = 0.4 V½, 2φF = 0.7 V. Find Vth for VSB = 1 V and 2 V.

VSB = 1 V: Vth = 0.5 + 0.4(√1.7 − √0.7) = 0.5 + 0.4(1.304 − 0.837) = 0.5 + 0.187 = 0.687 V.

VSB = 2 V: 0.5 + 0.4(√2.7 − 0.837) = 0.5 + 0.4(1.643 − 0.837) = 0.822 V. The rise is sub-linear (square root).

2. Channel-length modulation (CLM)

In saturation the pinch-off point moves toward the source as VDS rises (the drain depletion region "eats into" the channel), so the effective length becomes L − ΔL. A shorter channel carries more current (ID ∝ 1/L, your p.13), so the saturated curves tilt upward instead of being flat:

CLM (your p.13)
ID = 12 μnCox WL (VGS − Vth)² (1 + λVDS)
λ = CLM parameter (V-1)    VA = 1/λ (the MOSFET's "Early voltage")    ro = 1/(λID) = finite output resistance

The device is no longer an ideal current source. λ is larger (worse) for shorter channels, because the same ΔL is a bigger fraction of a small L. This is the exact twin of base-width modulation and the Early effect in the BJT (your set-A p.36).

Worked: an nMOS in saturation carries 1 mA at VDS = 1 V with λ = 0.1 V-1. Find the current at VDS = 3 V, VA and ro.
  1. 1 mA = I0(1 + 0.1 × 1) ⇒ I0 = 0.909 mA.
  2. At 3 V: ID = 0.909 × 1.3 = 1.18 mA (18 % more).
  3. VA = 1/λ = 10 V; ro ≈ 1/(λID) = 1/(0.1 × 1 mA) = 10 kΩ.

3. Velocity saturation

Recall Chapter 6: drift velocity vd = μE only at low fields; at high field it levels off at vsat (≈ 107 cm/s in Si) because scattering (optical phonons) balances the push. In a short channel, Ex = VDS/L is huge even for small VDS, so carriers hit vsat long before pinch-off. Your notes (p.13 to p.14):

Velocity saturation (your p.14)
vd = μE1 + E/Ec for E < Ec;   vd = vsat for E > Ec    (Ec = critical field, vsat ≈ μEc)
ID,short = μnCoxWL[(VGS − Vth)VDS − VDS²2] × 11 + VDS/(EcL)
Deep velocity saturation: ID ≈ W Cox vsat (VGS − Vth − VDSAT): linear in the overdrive, not squared.

Consequences (Drive MOSFET_3): VDSAT < VGS − Vth (the device saturates early), and ID becomes linear in (VGS − Vth) and almost independent of L. Shrinking L no longer increases the current as much as the long-channel formula promises.

Worked: μn = 400 cm²/V·s in the channel, vsat = 107 cm/s. Find Ec, and the current-reduction factor at VDS = 1 V for L = 1 μm and L = 100 nm.
  1. Ec = vsat/μ = 107/400 = 2.5×104 V/cm (2.5 V/μm).
  2. L = 1 μm: EcL = 2.5 V ⇒ factor 1/(1 + 1/2.5) = 0.71.
  3. L = 100 nm: EcL = 0.25 V ⇒ factor 1/(1 + 1/0.25) = 0.20: the current is only one fifth of the long-channel prediction.

4. Punch-through

The source–substrate and drain–substrate depletion regions grow toward each other. In a very short channel (or at high VDS) they touch, creating a direct path for electrons from source to drain under the gate. Current flows even when the device should be OFF, and the gate can no longer stop it. Remedy (Drive, doping notes): higher channel doping shortens the depletion widths and suppresses punch-through (and DIBL).

5. Drain-induced barrier lowering (DIBL)

Electrons in the source face a potential barrier (the hump in the right panel of the figure) that the gate controls. In a long channel only the gate sets this barrier. In a short channel the drain is close enough that a high VDS also pulls the barrier down. Lower barrier ⇒ easier to turn on ⇒ Vth falls as VDS rises (your p.14), so off-state leakage rises.

Beyond your notes

DIBL is usually modelled as Vth = Vth0 − ηDIBLVDS, with ηDIBL ≈ 0.05 to 0.15 V/V in short devices. Other short-channel effects you may meet: Vth roll-off (Vth falls as L shrinks), hot-carrier injection (energetic carriers damage the oxide), gate-oxide tunnelling (tox below ~2 nm, solved by high-k dielectrics, Chapter 14) and mobility degradation by the vertical field. FinFETs and nanosheet (gate-all-around) transistors wrap the gate around the channel to give the gate back its control.

Explain like I'm 10: the five effects in one story

The gate is a teacher controlling a doorway between two classrooms (source and drain). Body effect: the floor tilts, so the teacher must shout louder to open the door. CLM: the drain side keeps creeping closer, so the corridor gets shorter and a few more kids get through. Velocity saturation: kids can only run so fast, however steep the corridor. DIBL: the corridor is so short that the drain classroom's noise opens the door a little by itself. Punch-through: the two classrooms' walls collapse into each other and kids walk straight through, door or no door.

Exam traps for this chapter
  • Saturation in a MOSFET means current saturates (flat). In a BJT, "saturation" is the region where both junctions are forward-biased and the transistor is a closed switch. Don't mix them.
  • VDS,sat = VGS − Vth, not VGS.
  • Body effect: VSB ↑ ⇒ Vth ↑. DIBL: VDS ↑ ⇒ Vth ↓. Opposite directions, both asked.
  • CLM makes the curves slope up in saturation; it doesn't change the triode region formula (to first order).
  • Your p.14 writes the velocity-saturation factor as 1/(1 + VDS/Ec). Write 1/(1 + VDS/(EcL)): VDS/L is the field.
  • The sub-threshold slope can never be below 60 mV/decade at 300 K for a normal MOSFET; "lower S" means a better (sharper) switch.

CHAPTER 12The CMOS Inverter and Static CMOS Logic

The inverter is the "main workout" of digital VLSI (your Drive's words). Master its structure, switch model, static behaviour, VTC, noise margins, delay and power, then build NAND, NOR and any gate from it.

Your class notes 1-10-26 and two notebook photos Drive: CMOS_1; board notes 1112-1600 (static CMOS design)

12.1 Structure: pull-up and pull-down

  • M2 = pMOS, source to VDD: the pull-up network (PUN). It can connect the output to logic 1.
  • M1 = nMOS, source to GND: the pull-down network (PDN). It can connect the output to logic 0.
  • The two gates are tied together to Vin; the two drains are tied together to Vout; Cload hangs from Vout to ground.
  • Logic levels: 0 = GND, 1 = VDD. This is static CMOS technology.
  • Device reminders from your notes: the nMOS is an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, ON for VGS > Vtn (positive). The pMOS is a p-channel enhancement MOSFET (p⁺ source/drain in an n-substrate or n-well), ON for VGS < Vtp (negative), i.e. when its gate is at least |Vtp| below its source.
Case (your notes)VinnMOS M1: VGSnpMOS M2: VGSpM1M2Vout
10 V (logic 0)0 < Vtn−VDD (very negative)OFFONVDD (logic 1); M2 charges CL
2VDD (logic 1)VDD > Vtn0ONOFF0 (logic 0); M1 discharges CL
Explain like I'm 10

A see-saw with two doors. One door opens to a room full of "1"s (VDD), the other to a room full of "0"s (ground). The input pushes the see-saw: push down (input 0) and the top door opens, so the output fills up to 1. Push up (input 1) and the bottom door opens, so the output drains to 0. Because the see-saw can never have both doors open at rest, water never pours straight from the top room to the bottom room. That's why CMOS wastes almost no power when it is just sitting there.

12.2 The switch model and delay

Your photo and the Drive replace each transistor with a switch in series with its on-resistance (Chapter 11, Ron):

  • Vin = 0: pMOS = resistor Rp from VDD to Vout; nMOS = open switch. CL charges up through Rp.
  • Vin = VDD: pMOS open; nMOS = resistor Rn to ground. CL discharges through Rn.

Your notes say "you can calculate the time constant": each case is a first-order RC circuit (the Drive: "first-order ODE").

Delay of the inverter
Discharge: Vout(t) = VDD e−t/RnCL    time constant τn = RnCL (high to low)
Charge: Vout(t) = VDD(1 − e−t/RpCL)    τp = RpCL (low to high)
Time to reach 50 %: e−t/τ = ½ ⇒ t = τ ln 2 = 0.69τ  ⇒  tpHL = 0.69RnCL, tpLH = 0.69RpCL, tp = (tpHL + tpLH)/2

What is CL? (Drive) The internal capacitances of the inverter itself (the gate–drain and drain–body capacitances of both transistors), the wiring, and the input (gate) capacitance of every gate it drives.

Worked: Rn = 5 kΩ, Rp = 10 kΩ, CL = 20 fF. Find tpHL, tpLH, tp. How should the pMOS be resized to equalise them?
  1. tpHL = 0.69 × 5 kΩ × 20 fF = 69 ps.
  2. tpLH = 0.69 × 10 kΩ × 20 fF = 138 ps.
  3. tp = (69 + 138)/2 = 103.5 ps.
  4. R ∝ L/W, so doubling the pMOS width halves Rp to 5 kΩ and makes tpLH = 69 ps (ignoring the extra capacitance the wider pMOS adds).

12.3 Static behaviour: the three properties in your notes

  1. Zero (very small) static power dissipation. In either steady state one transistor is OFF, so there is no DC path from VDD to GND. Only tiny leakage (sub-threshold, junction) flows.
  2. High input impedance. The input drives only gates, and the gate oxide is an insulator: no DC input current. Hence the Drive's static fan-out is ideally infinite: one inverter could hold any number of following gates at the right DC level. But every extra gate adds capacitance, so the dynamic fan-out is limited by speed.
  3. Low output impedance. The output is always connected to VDD or GND through an ON transistor (a few kΩ). It is "stiff": noise injected onto the output is quickly pulled back, giving good noise immunity.

The Drive adds a fourth: ratioless logic with full (rail-to-rail) swing. VOH = VDD and VOL = 0 exactly, whatever the W/L of the two transistors. (Sizing changes speed and the switching point, not the final levels.) The pseudo-nMOS gate of §12.7 is ratioed: its VOL depends on the size ratio.

12.4 The voltage transfer characteristic (VTC)

The VTC is Vout plotted against Vin as Vin sweeps 0 → VDD (your notes: the curve falls from VDD to 0). To find any point, use the Drive's rule: the same current flows through both transistors (IDn = IDp, a load-line intersection), with

VGSn = Vin,   VDSn = Vout,   VGSp = Vin − VDD,   VDSp = Vout − VDD
RegionVin rangenMOSpMOSVout
A0 to Vtncut-offlinear (Rp)VDD
BVtn to just below VMsaturationlinearslightly below VDD, falling
C≈ VMsaturationsaturationdrops steeply (highest gain)
Djust above VM to VDD − |Vtp|linearsaturationsmall, falling
EVDD − |Vtp| to VDDlinear (Rn)cut-off0

Switching threshold VM

Your notes: VM is where the VTC crosses the line Vout = Vin. At that point both transistors are in saturation, so equate the two saturation currents with Vin = Vout = VM:

  1. ½kn(VM − Vtn)² = ½kp(VDD − VM − |Vtp|)², where kn = μnCox(W/L)n, kp = μpCox(W/L)p.
  2. Take square roots with r = √(kp/kn): VM − Vtn = r(VDD − VM − |Vtp|).
  3. Solve: VM = Vtn + r(VDD −Vtp|)|1 + r

If kn = kp (r = 1) and Vtn = |Vtp|, then VM = VDD/2: a symmetric inverter. Since μn ≈ 2 to 3 μp, this needs (W/L)p = (μn/μp)(W/L)n ≈ 2 to 3 × (W/L)n. A stronger nMOS pulls VM down; a stronger pMOS pushes it up.

Worked: VDD = 1.8 V, Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.4 V, μnCox = 200 μA/V², μpCox = 80 μA/V², (W/L)n = 2. Find VM for (W/L)p = 2, and the (W/L)p for VM = 0.9 V.
  1. kn = 400 μA/V²; kp = 160 μA/V² ⇒ r = √0.4 = 0.632.
  2. VM = (0.4 + 0.632 × 1.4)/1.632 = (0.4 + 0.885)/1.632 = 0.79 V (below VDD/2: the nMOS is stronger).
  3. For VM = VDD/2 we need r = 1, kp = kn: 80 × (W/L)p = 400 ⇒ (W/L)p = 5 = 2.5 × (W/L)n.

Noise margins

Real signals carry noise (the Drive lists 1/f, shot, wiring and junction noise). The inverter must still read a slightly wrong "0" as 0 and a slightly wrong "1" as 1. The boundaries are the two points where the VTC slope is −1:

Noise margins
VIL = largest input still read as 0    VIH = smallest input read as 1    (both at dVout/dVin = −1)
NML = VIL − VOL     NMH = VOH − VIH    (CMOS: VOH = VDD, VOL = 0)
Beyond your notes: closed forms for a matched inverter (kn = kp, Vtn = |Vtp| = Vt)
VIL = 3VDD + 2Vt8    VIH = 5VDD − 2Vt8    NML = NMH = 3VDD + 2Vt8

Derivation sketch for VIL: in region B the nMOS is saturated and the pMOS linear. Write ½k(Vin − Vt)² = k[(VDD − Vin − Vt)(VDD − Vout) − ½(VDD − Vout)²], differentiate with respect to Vin, set dVout/dVin = −1, and solve the two equations together. VIH follows by symmetry. Example: VDD = 1.8 V, Vt = 0.4 V ⇒ VIL = 0.775 V, VIH = 1.025 V, both margins 0.775 V (43 % of VDD).

Gain

Gain Av = dVout/dVin is the slope of the VTC, largest (most negative) at VM. Your photo example: Av = 100, so a 10-3 V change at the input gives ΔVout = 100 × 10-3 = 0.1 V (in magnitude; the output moves the opposite way). The Drive's point: high gain makes the transition sharp, which gives large noise margins and fast regeneration of degraded logic levels; biased at VM, the inverter is also an analog amplifier.

12.5 Power dissipation

CMOS power
Dynamic: each 0 → 1 → 0 cycle takes CLVDD² from the supply (½CLVDD² burnt in the pMOS while charging, ½ stored then burnt in the nMOS while discharging) ⇒ Pdyn = α CL VDD² f (α = activity factor, fraction of cycles that switch)
Short-circuit: while Vin is between Vtn and VDD − |Vtp|, both devices conduct (the spike in the right panel of the figure). Small if input edges are fast.
Static: leakage only, Pstat = IleakVDD (sub-threshold, Chapter 11, plus junction leakage).

Because Pdyn ∝ VDD², lowering the supply is the most powerful way to save power; that is why supplies fell from 5 V to about 1 V.

Worked: an inverter drives 50 fF at 500 MHz with VDD = 1.8 V and switches every cycle (α = 1). Find the dynamic power. What if VDD is cut to 1.2 V?

P = 50×10-15 × 1.8² × 5×108 = 50×10-15 × 3.24 × 5×108 = 81 μW. At 1.2 V: × (1.2/1.8)² = × 0.444 ⇒ 36 μW (56 % less).

12.6 Sizing for equal rise and fall (board notes)

The board notes define tPLH (output 0 → 1) and tPHL (1 → 0) and design for tPLH = tPHL. Equal delays need equal resistances, i.e. equal current drive:

μnCox(W/L)n = μpCox(W/L)p  ⇒  (W/L)p = μnμp (W/L)n ≈ 2 to 3 × (W/L)n

This is the same condition as VM = VDD/2 above: a symmetric inverter is symmetric in both its VTC and its timing.

12.7 Static CMOS gates: the design method

The method from your board notes
  1. Design the PDN (nMOS) from the un-inverted function: an OR (A + B) = nMOS in parallel; an AND (AB) = nMOS in series. The PDN conducts (pulls Y to 0) exactly when the function inside the bar is 1.
  2. The PUN (pMOS) is the dual: every parallel connection in the PDN becomes series in the PUN, and every series becomes parallel. The same input drives one nMOS and one pMOS.
  3. The output is the inverted function. Static CMOS can only make inverting gates directly (NAND, NOR, AOI, OAI). An AND = NAND + inverter.

An N-input static CMOS gate uses 2N transistors. At every input combination exactly one of PUN/PDN conducts, so the gate keeps all the inverter's properties: no static current and full swing.

Example 1: 2-input NOR, Y = (A + B)′

PDN: M3 (A) ∥ M4 (B). PUN: M1 (A) in series with M2 (B).

ABONY
00M1, M2 (path to VDD); M3, M4 off1
01M4 (path to GND); M2 off0
10M3; M1 off0
11M3, M4; M1, M2 off0

Example 2: 2-input NAND, Y = (AB)′

PUN: M1 (A) ∥ M2 (B). PDN: M3 (A) in series with M4 (B).

ABONY
00M1, M21
01M1 (and M4, but M3 open)1
10M2 (and M3, but M4 open)1
11M3, M4 (series path to GND)0

Example 3 (board): Y = (AB + CD)′. PDN: (A series B) in parallel with (C series D). PUN, the dual: (A ∥ B) in series with (C ∥ D). 8 transistors. Check: A = B = 1 turns on the A–B nMOS chain ⇒ Y = 0; at the same time pMOS A and B are both off, so the upper PUN block is open ⇒ no path to VDD. ✓

Pseudo-nMOS technique (board): replace the whole PUN with a single pMOS whose gate is grounded (always ON) and keep the nMOS PDN. A 2-input NOR then needs 3 transistors instead of 4 (N + 1 instead of 2N). The cost: whenever the PDN is ON, current flows straight from VDD to GND through the always-on pMOS (static power), and VOL is not 0 but set by the pMOS/nMOS resistance ratio (ratioed logic). The 4×4 NOR ROM in Chapter 16 uses exactly this pull-up.

Beyond your notes: sizing gates for equal delay

Series transistors add their resistances. To make a NAND as fast as a reference inverter with (W/L)n = 1 and (W/L)p = 2.5, the two series nMOS must each be twice as wide (W/L = 2); the parallel pMOS can stay at 2.5 (worst case is only one of them ON). For a NOR, the two series pMOS must each be 5. Large series pMOS stacks are slow and big, which is why NAND gates are preferred over NOR gates in CMOS.

Practice: design Y = (A(B + C))′. Give the PDN, the PUN, the transistor count and the output for A = 1, B = 0, C = 1.
  1. Inside the bar: A AND (B OR C). PDN: nMOS A in series with (nMOS B ∥ nMOS C).
  2. PUN (dual): pMOS A in parallel with (pMOS B in series with pMOS C).
  3. 6 transistors (3 inputs × 2).
  4. A = 1, B = 0, C = 1: nMOS A on and nMOS C on ⇒ path to GND ⇒ Y = 0. Check the PUN: pMOS A off, and the B–C series pair is broken because pMOS C is off ⇒ no path to VDD. ✓ (A(B + C) = 1 ⇒ Y = 0.)
Practice: how many transistors does a static CMOS 3-input NOR need? Which network has the series stack, and why is it the slow one?

6 transistors. The PUN has three pMOS in series (the PDN has three nMOS in parallel). Series resistances add, and pMOS already has the lower mobility, so the 0 → 1 output transition through three series pMOS is the slowest. To compensate each pMOS would need to be about 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 times the unit nMOS width.

Exam traps
  • pMOS is the pull-up (to VDD); nMOS is the pull-down. pMOS passes a strong 1, nMOS passes a strong 0.
  • VM is where Vout = Vin, not where Vout = VDD/2 (they coincide only for a symmetric inverter).
  • In the PDN, AND ⇒ series, OR ⇒ parallel. The PUN is the dual, not a copy.
  • "Zero static power" means no DC current at rest. Power is still burnt every time the output switches: αCVDD²f.
  • Noise margins use the slope = −1 points, not the threshold VM.
  • Delay to 50 % is 0.69RC, not RC (RC is the 63 % time).

CHAPTER 13Unit I and the MOS Capacitor: Everything Extra in the Drive

Chapters 1 to 9 cover what was written on the board. The instructor's typed Drive notes go further in many places. This chapter adds every one of those extras, in syllabus order, so nothing in the Drive can surprise you.

Drive: Unit I files 1 to 14; MOS Capacitor_1, MOS Capacitor_2

13.1 Crystals, Brillouin zone and band structure vs band diagram

  • Only a crystalline material (atoms repeating periodically in x, y, z) has a well-defined band gap. A completely full valence band carries no current, because there are no empty states for electrons to move into.
  • Example gaps from the Drive: metals have no gap (Au, Ag, Zn); an insulator ≈ 8 eV (Al2O3; SiO2 ≈ 9 eV); Si 1.1, Ge 0.7 eV. Room-temperature kT = 0.0259 eV.
  • E = ħ²k²/2m is exact only for a free electron in vacuum. In a crystal the periodic potential (solved with the Schrödinger equation) distorts the parabola and opens gaps at k = ±π/a, ±2π/a, … (Chapter 2 figure). The range −π/a ≤ k ≤ +π/a is the first Brillouin zone; everything else repeats it. Near k = 0 the band is still roughly parabolic, which is why the effective mass works.
  • Why m* matters (Drive): it packs all the quantum mechanics into one number so we can use plain F = ma for electrons in a crystal. Higher curvature ⇒ lower m* ⇒ higher mobility ⇒ higher current and higher speed.
  • Band structure (E vs k) shows allowed energies against momentum: used for direct/indirect gaps and m*. Band diagram (E vs x) shows Ec, Ev, EF against position in a device: used for junctions and MOS. Don't mix the two pictures.
  • Direct gap materials (GaAs, GaN) have a high absorption coefficient and emit light efficiently. Indirect ones (Si, Ge) need a phonon, so they absorb weakly and hardly emit; Si solar cells still work, they just need to be thicker.
  • Moore's law (Drive, file 1): transistor count per chip doubles about every two years while the cost per transistor falls.

13.2 Density of states and the carrier integrals

Your notes (set A p.8) wrote n = ∫ g(E) f(E) dE. The Drive gives the actual shapes:

Density of states (states per eV per cm³)
gc(E) = 4π(2mn*)3/2h³ √(E − Ec) for E ≥ Ec     gv(E) = 4π(2mp*)3/2h³ √(Ev − E) for E ≤ Ev
Inside the gap g = 0, so there are no electrons there even where f = 0.5.

Doing the integral gives n = NcF1/2(η), where F1/2 is the Fermi–Dirac integral of order ½. If EF is at least 3kT away from the band edge, the Fermi function's tail is a plain exponential (the Boltzmann approximation) and the integral becomes simple:

Non-degenerate carrier concentrations
n = Nc exp[−(Ec − EF)/kT]     p = Nv exp[−(EF − Ev)/kT]
Effective densities of states: Nc = 2(2πmn*kT/h²)3/2, Nv = 2(2πmp*kT/h²)3/2; Si at 300 K: Nc ≈ 2.8×1019, Nv ≈ 1.04×1019 cm-3 (both ∝ T3/2)
Multiply: np = NcNve−Eg/kT = ni² ⇒ ni = √(NcNv) exp(−Eg/2kT) (this is why mass action holds)
Worked: (a) compute ni for Si. (b) Where is EF in Si with n = 1016 cm-3? Is the Boltzmann approximation valid?

(a) √(2.8×1019 × 1.04×1019) = 1.71×1019; Eg/2kT = 1.12/0.0518 = 21.6; e−21.6 = 4.1×10-10 ⇒ ni ≈ 7×109 cm-3. Textbooks quote 1×1010 or 1.5×1010 depending on the m* and Eg values used; use whatever the question gives.

(b) Ec − EF = kT ln(Nc/n) = 0.0259 × ln(2800) = 0.0259 × 7.94 = 0.206 eV below Ec. That is 8kT > 3kT ⇒ Boltzmann is fine.

The Drive stresses that ni cannot be reduced: it is the minimum carrier concentration that heat always creates. Higher ni means more leakage current and noise: Ge (0.68 eV) is leaky, GaN (3.4 eV) has a vanishingly small ni.

13.3 Temperature: freeze-out, extrinsic, intrinsic

  1. Freeze-out (≈ 10 to 50 K up to ~100 K): kT ≪ Ec − ED, so donors keep their electrons; n falls exponentially as T drops.
  2. Extrinsic (includes room temperature): donors ~100 % ionised, n ≈ ND, independent of T. This is the region devices are designed for.
  3. Intrinsic (very high T; for Si roughly 500 to 700 °C at moderate doping): ni ∝ e−Eg/2kT outgrows ND; the doping no longer controls the conductivity. Wide-gap GaN and SiC stay extrinsic to much higher temperatures, so they are used for hot, high-power electronics.

13.4 Heavy doping and incomplete ionisation

  • Degenerate semiconductor: at very high doping EF comes within 3kT (≈ 78 meV at 300 K) of the band edge or even enters the band (EF > Ec). The Boltzmann formula fails. The Drive gives the Joyce–Dixon approximation: (EF − Ec)/kT = ln(n/Nc) + (1/√8)(n/Nc), solved numerically.
  • Band-gap narrowing: heavy doping distorts the lattice potential so Eg shrinks (Si 1.1 → ~1.0 eV) and the band edges grow band tails.
  • Incomplete ionisation: a dopant is fully ionised only if its level is within about kT of the band. At 3 to 4 kT it is only partly ionised. Example from the Drive: Mg acceptors in GaN are only 1 to 5 % ionised (1017 Mg gives about 1015 holes), a real problem for blue/white LEDs.
Ionisation fractions
ND+ND = 11 + 2 exp[(EF − ED)/kT] (factor 2: spin)     NA−NA = 11 + 4 exp[(EA − EF)/kT] (factor 4: spin × heavy/light holes)
Charge neutrality must use the ionised numbers: p + ND+ = n + NA−.
Worked: what fraction of donors is ionised when EF = ED? When EF is 3kT below ED? When 2kT above?

EF = ED: 1/(1 + 2) = 33 % (the Drive's number). 3kT below: 1/(1 + 2e−3) = 91 %. 2kT above: 1/(1 + 2e2) = 6 %.

13.5 Scattering and mobility, the details

  • Scattering is not a billiard-ball hit: a disturbance in the periodic potential deflects the electron. Two sources: phonons (lattice vibrations; modes are acoustic and optical, each transverse and longitudinal), stronger at high T; and ionised impurities (Coulomb), stronger at low T and high doping.
  • The drift cycle: accelerate, gain energy, scatter, lose energy, repeat. Velocity = random thermal part (no current) + drift part (only with a field; the field can be internal, from a band slope).
  • μ = qτ/m* (cm²/V·s): mobility is the slope of v vs E, ∝ τ and ∝ 1/m* (holes are heavier, so slower).
  • Low field: v = μE. High field: v saturates, dv/dE = 0, and mobility no longer matters. Many short-channel transistors work in this regime (Chapter 11).
  • The Drive warns that this temperature dependence matters for design: CMOS logic timing can fail when mobility drops on a hot chip.
Worked: electrons in Si have μn = 1350 cm²/V·s and m* = 0.26m0. Find the mean time between collisions.

τ = μm*/q = (0.135 m²/V·s × 0.26 × 9.11×10-31 kg)/1.6×10-19 C = 2.0×10-13 s = 0.2 ps. (Convert μ to SI first: 1350 cm²/V·s = 0.135 m²/V·s.)

13.6 Einstein's relation: the derivation, and the built-in field of non-uniform doping

Your notes state Dn/μn = kT/q. The Drive derives it:

  1. Take an n-type bar in equilibrium whose doping falls from left to right. EF is flat (equilibrium), so Ec − EF grows to the right: the bands tilt.
  2. A tilted band means a field: E = (1/q) dEc/dx (as on your set-A p.23). This is the built-in field of non-uniform doping.
  3. n(x) = Nc exp[(EF − Ec(x))/kT] ⇒ dn/dx = −(n/kT) dEc/dx.
  4. In equilibrium the total current is zero, so drift balances diffusion in magnitude: qDn|dn/dx| = qμnnE ⇒ qDn(n/kT)(dEc/dx) = μnn(dEc/dx).
  5. Cancel: Dn/μn = kT/q. Although derived at equilibrium, it holds generally.

13.7 Traps and Shockley–Read–Hall statistics

Physical defects (dislocations, missing lines of atoms, vacancies, dangling bonds, impurities, interstitials) create discrete states at ET inside the gap. They matter in p–n junctions, BJTs, LEDs and solar cells. Four processes happen at a trap:

ProcessWhat happensRate (Drive)
raelectron capture (CB → empty trap)σnvthnNt(1 − f)
rbelectron emission (full trap → CB)enNtf
rchole capture (full trap's electron drops to VB)σpvthpNtf
rdhole emission (VB electron jumps up to the empty trap)epNt(1 − f)

σ = capture cross-section (cm²), vth = thermal velocity (≈ 107 cm/s), so σvth is the volume an electron sweeps per second; f = trap occupancy (a Fermi function at Et). In steady state ra − rb = rc − rd, and solving gives your SRH formula U = (pn − ni²)/[τ(p + n + 2ni)] for mid-gap traps, with

τ = 1σ vth Nt    more traps ⇒ shorter lifetime ⇒ faster recombination. (The Drive writes n for the density; physically it is the trap density Nt.)

Recombination can be radiative (energy leaves as light, band-to-band in direct-gap materials) or non-radiative (energy leaves as heat/phonons, typical of traps).

Worked: σ = 10-15 cm², vth = 107 cm/s, Nt = 1014 cm-3. Find τ. What happens if contamination raises Nt to 1016?

τ = 1/(10-15 × 107 × 1014) = 1 μs. At Nt = 1016: τ = 10 ns, 100× shorter. This is why fabs fight metal contamination.

13.8 Optical generation and the continuity equation

A photon can create an electron–hole pair only if its energy reaches the gap: hν = hc/λ ≥ Eg ⇒ λ ≤ hc/Eg (cut-off wavelength). Handy form: λ(μm) = 1.24/Eg(eV). Si: 1.24/1.12 = 1.1 μm, so Si detects visible and near-IR light. GL = optical generation rate (cm-3s-1).

The continuity equation is bookkeeping for a thin slice A·dx: (rate of change of carriers) = (flow in − flow out) + (generation) − (recombination):

Continuity equation (electrons)
∂n∂t = 1q ∂Jn∂x + GL − U    (for minority electrons in p-type, U = Δn/τ)
Steady state, no field (diffusion only): Dn d²Δndx² + GL − Δnτ = 0
With GL = 0: d²Δn/dx² = Δn/Ln²,   Ln = √(Dnτn)  ⇒  Δn(x) = A1ex/Ln + A2e−x/Ln
  • Example 1, uniform illumination (no gradient, steady): GL = Δn/τ ⇒ Δn = GLτ.
  • Example 2, light switched off at t = 0 (uniform): dΔn/dt = −Δn/τ ⇒ Δn(t) = GLτ e−t/τ. Watching this decay is how lifetime is measured.
  • Ln is the average distance an excess electron diffuses before it recombines; it is the Ln, Lp in your diode current (set A p.26).
Worked: p-type Si, μn = 1350 cm²/V·s, τn = 1 μs, uniformly lit with GL = 1020 cm-3s-1. Find Δn, Dn, Ln, and Δn 2 μs after the light goes off.
  1. Δn = GLτ = 1020 × 10-6 = 1014 cm-3.
  2. Dn = μnkT/q = 1350 × 0.0259 = 35 cm²/s.
  3. Ln = √(35 × 10-6) = 5.9×10-3 cm = 59 μm.
  4. After 2 μs = 2τ: Δn = 1014 e−2 = 1.35×1013 cm-3.

13.9 The p–n junction in equilibrium: derivations

Assumptions (Drive): moderate doping (no band tails or Joyce–Dixon), full ionisation, no light or external fields, and the depletion approximation (absolutely no mobile carriers inside W, perfectly neutral outside). The neutral regions have no field; EF is constant everywhere, which forces the bands to bend.

Explain like I'm 10: the "cemented floor" (Drive)

Imagine Ec is a floor made of cement. Electrons are marbles that roll downhill on it. Across the junction the floor slopes down toward the n-side, so marbles that wander to the p-side roll back. The slope is the built-in field (pointing n → p), and its height is qVbi. Holes are bubbles that float up the Ev floor, so they are pushed back to the p-side.

Built-in voltage, the Drive's derivation
n-side: Ec − EF = kT ln(Nc/ND)    p-side: EF − Ev = kT ln(Nv/NA)
qVbi = Eg − (Ec − EF)n − (EF − Ev)p = Eg − kT ln[NcNv/(NAND)]
Use ni² = NcNve−Eg/kT ⇒ ln(NcNv) = ln ni² + Eg/kT; the Eg terms cancel ⇒ Vbi = (kT/q) ln(NAND/ni²) (your set-A p.21 formula)
More doping or a wider gap (smaller ni) ⇒ larger Vbi; maximum ≈ Eg/q at degenerate doping. Vbi cannot be measured with a voltmeter (contact potentials cancel it).
Poisson's equation and the field (n-side, 0 ≤ x ≤ Wn)
d²V/dx² = −ρ/εs with ρ = qND ⇒ field is a straight line: |E(x)| = qNDεs(Wn − x), zero at the depletion edge
|Emax| = qNDWnεs = qNAWpεs at the junction (x = 0)    ⇒ NAWp = NDWn
Potential drops: Vn = qNDWn²/2εs, Vp = qNAWp²/2εs, Vbi = Vn + Vp = ½|Emax|W ⇒ the W formula of your set-A p.22
Worked: Si p⁺n junction, NA = 1017, ND = 1015 cm-3, ni = 1.5×1010. Find Vbi, W, Wn, Wp, Emax, and W at 5 V reverse bias.
  1. Vbi = 0.0259 ln(1032/2.25×1020) = 0.0259 × 26.82 = 0.695 V.
  2. W = √[(2 × 1.04×10-12 × 0.695/1.6×10-19)(10-17 + 10-15)] = √(9.13×10-9) = 0.955 μm.
  3. Wn = W·NA/(NA + ND) = 0.946 μm; Wp = 9.5 nm: the depletion lies almost entirely in the lightly doped side.
  4. Emax = 2Vbi/W = 1.39/9.55×10-5 = 1.45×104 V/cm.
  5. At VR = 5 V replace Vbi by Vbi + VR = 5.695 V: W = 0.955 × √(5.695/0.695) = 2.73 μm.

Very high doping on both sides (≈ 1018 and above) makes W only 10 to 20 nm, thin enough for electrons to tunnel straight through: the tunnel diode.

13.10 The biased junction: quasi-Fermi levels, long and short diodes

  • Under bias there is no single EF. Each carrier type gets its own quasi-Fermi level, EFn and EFp. Their separation across the junction equals qVa; they merge into one EF at Va = 0. In general np = ni² e(EFn − EFp)/kT, which is where your pn(xn) = pn0eV/VT comes from.
  • Barrier under bias: q(Vbi − Va). Drive example: 0.76 − 0.4 = 0.36 V forward; 0.76 + 2 = 2.76 V at 2 V reverse.
  • Long diode (neutral region ≫ Lp): excess carriers decay exponentially, as in your notes. Short diode (neutral region ≪ Lp): almost no recombination, so the profile is a straight line and Lp is replaced by the region length in J0. The BJT base is a short diode.
  • Total current is the same at every x (Kirchhoff). Far from the junction the minority diffusion current has died away, so the current is carried by majority-carrier drift in the quasi-neutral regions. That's why your notes (p.27) add the drift picture.
  • J0 ∝ ni²: Ge leaks a lot, GaN very little, so wide-gap diodes are better rectifiers (power devices, low dark current in photodetectors). In reverse bias the minority concentration at the depletion edge is ≈ 0; the tiny J0 is made of thermally generated minority carriers that wander to the edge and are swept across.

13.11 Generation–recombination currents and the ideality factor

The ideal-diode law assumed no recombination inside the depletion region. Real junctions contain traps there, where p and n are both small, which is exactly where SRH is most effective. So Jtotal = Jideal + JGR. Sign of U: U > 0 = net recombination (forward bias); U < 0 = net generation (reverse bias).

Recombination current (forward)
Assume mid-gap traps and p ≈ n at the worst point; with pn = ni²eqVa/kT ⇒ p ≈ n ≈ nieqVa/2kT
Umax ≈ ni²eqV/kTτ · 2nieqV/2kT = ni2τ eqV/2kT  ⇒  Jrec ≈ qniW2τ eqVa/2kT
Generation current (reverse)
p, n ≪ ni ⇒ U ≈ −ni/2τ (net generation from traps, not light) ⇒ Jgen = qniW2τ    Jrev = −(J0 + Jgen)
Jgen ∝ W ∝ √(Vbi + VR), so real reverse current creeps up with VR until breakdown.
Ideality factor η
J ∝ eqV/ηkT: ideal diffusion η = 1; recombination η = 2. Low V: Jrec dominates (slope 1/2kT on a log plot). High V: diffusion dominates (slope 1/kT). Poor material (badly grown GaN) can show η = 5 to 10.
Worked: the diode of §13.9 (W = 0.955 μm at zero bias; say 0.5 μm effective) with τ = 1 μs. Compare Jgen with the diffusion J0 (hole side: Dp = 12 cm²/s, Lp = √(Dpτ)).
  1. Jgen = qniW/2τ = 1.6×10-19 × 1×1010 × 0.5×10-4 / 2×10-6 = 4×10-8 A/cm² (using ni = 1010).
  2. Lp = √(12 × 10-6) = 34.6 μm. J0 ≈ qni²Dp/(LpND) = 1.6×10-19 × 1020 × 12/(3.46×10-3 × 1015) = 5.5×10-11 A/cm².
  3. Jgen/J0 ≈ 700. In silicon at room temperature the real reverse current is mostly generation current, because Jgen ∝ ni while J0 ∝ ni².
Material (Drive)Eg (eV)Turn-on voltage ≈ Vbi
Ge0.7~0.4 V
Si1.10.7 to 0.8 V
GaAs1.421.0 to 1.1 V
GaN3.4~3.2 V

This table is the answer to your Si-vs-Ge assignment (set A p.30) in numbers: the same 20 mA needs more voltage (and more power) in a wider-gap diode.

13.12 Breakdown, in depth

  • Breakdown happens only in reverse, where almost the whole voltage drops across the depletion region. It is not destructive unless the current is allowed to grow without limit (Zener diodes work there on purpose).
  • Zener (tunnelling): both sides heavily doped ⇒ W very thin ⇒ VB electrons on the p-side tunnel straight into empty CB states on the n-side through a thin triangular barrier. VBR ≲ 4Eg/q (≈ 4.4 V for Si; your notes: < 5 V).
  • Avalanche (impact ionisation): lighter doping, wider W; a carrier gains enough energy to knock a new electron–hole pair out of the lattice, and the new carriers do the same: a chain reaction. VBR ≳ 6Eg/q (> 6.6 V for Si; your notes: > 8 V). The most common mechanism.
  • Impact-ionisation coefficient αn = (1/n)(dn/dx) (new pairs per cm). Multiplication factor M = 1/(1 − ∫0Wα dx); breakdown when the integral reaches 1 (M → ∞).
  • Critical field Fcrit: Si ≈ 4×105 V/cm, GaN ≈ 3×106 V/cm, weakly dependent on doping. The field is triangular, so VBR = ½ W Fmax. For W = 1 μm: Si ½ × 10-4 × 4×105 = 20 V; GaN ≈ 150 V (the Drive quotes 180 V with a slightly larger Fcrit). That is why GaN and SiC are used for high-power switches.
Worked: one-sided Si junction with ND = 1016 cm-3 on the light side. Estimate the avalanche breakdown voltage.

At breakdown Emax = qNDW/εs = Fcrit and VBR = ½WFcrit ⇒ VBR = εsFcrit²/(2qND) = 1.04×10-12 × (4×105)²/(2 × 1.6×10-19 × 1016) = 52 V. Lighter doping ⇒ higher breakdown voltage.

13.13 Junction capacitance and C–V profiling

The depletion region is a parallel-plate capacitor whose gap W changes with voltage: Cj = εsA/W = ΔQ/ΔV. Reverse bias ↑ ⇒ W ↑ ⇒ C ↓ (the basis of the varactor). For a one-sided p⁺n junction, putting W into C gives a straight line:

C–V profiling (per unit area)
1C² = 2(Vbi − VA)qεsND    |slope| = 2/(qεsND) ⇒ ND of the lightly doped side    intercept on the V axis ⇒ Vbi
(If C is the total capacitance, put A² in the denominator: 1/C² = 2(Vbi − VA)/(qεsNDA²).)

13.14 One junction, four jobs: LED, photodetector, solar cell

QuadrantBiasDeviceKey facts
Q1forwardLEDNeeds a direct gap (GaAs, GaN; not Si or Ge). Radiative band-to-band recombination emits λ = hc/Eg ≈ 1242/Eg nm (Eg in eV). Bias slightly above turn-on (e.g. 2.2 to 2.3 V for a 2 V LED). Simple junctions are inefficient: carriers cross too fast and the p and n regions re-absorb photons; fix with wider-gap cladding layers.
Q2—not used
Q3reverse (or zero), litPhotodetectorA photon with E ≥ Eg makes a pair in the depletion region; the field sweeps the electron to n and the hole to p. Dark current = J0 + generation; signal = photocurrent; sensitivity = photo/dark ratio. Biased near breakdown it multiplies its own current: the avalanche photodiode (APD).
Q4self-biased by a loadSolar cellSame mechanism, but the cell delivers power, like a battery. ISC = short-circuit current (at V = 0, equal to the photocurrent); VOC = open-circuit voltage; efficiency from the maximum-power point (fill factor). Sunlight peaks around 500 to 550 nm, so choose the gap to match.
Worked: (a) emission wavelength of GaN and GaAs LEDs. (b) A solar cell has I0 = 1 pA and Iph = 2 mA. Find VOC.

(a) GaN: 1242/3.4 = 365 nm (near-UV/violet; the Drive's number). GaAs: 1242/1.42 = 875 nm (infrared). Wider gap ⇒ shorter wavelength ⇒ higher turn-on voltage.

(b) At open circuit the net current is zero: I0(eV/VT − 1) = Iph ⇒ VOC = VT ln(Iph/I0 + 1) = 0.0259 × ln(2×109) = 0.0259 × 21.4 = 0.555 V.

13.15 The MOS capacitor in band-diagram language

  • Ideal flat band: metal and semiconductor work functions equal (φm = φs), so at VG = 0 the Fermi levels line up and the bands are flat. A gate voltage separates the two Fermi levels by qVG.
  • Bulk potential φF (ψBP): qφF = Ei − EF in the bulk, a measure of how p-type the substrate is: φF = VT ln(NA/ni).
  • Accumulation (VG < 0): holes pile up, bands bend up at the surface (Ev moves toward EF).
  • Depletion (small VG > 0): holes pushed away, bands bend down; the surface becomes less p-type.
  • Weak inversion starts when Ei at the surface reaches EF (band bending = φF: surface is intrinsic).
  • Strong inversion: Ei at the surface is φF below EF, so the surface is as n-type as the bulk is p-type. Total band bending ψs = 2φF. This is the threshold condition used in Chapter 9.
  • Flat-band voltage VFB: in a real device (φm ≠ φs, charge in the oxide) the bands are not flat at zero bias; VFB is the gate voltage that flattens them. Vth = VFB + 2φF + Qd/Cox.
The C–V curve, all four cases (MOS Capacitor_2)
  • C is measured with a small AC signal on top of the DC bias: C = ΔQ/ΔV.
  • Accumulation: majority holes respond instantly at the interface ⇒ C = Cox (the maximum).
  • Depletion: Cdep = εs/WD in series with Cox; VG ↑ ⇒ WD ↑ ⇒ C ↓.
  • Strong inversion: WD stops at WD,max (the inversion layer screens the field) ⇒ Cmin. Low frequency (~100 Hz): minority electrons have time to be generated and follow the signal ⇒ C climbs back to Cox. High frequency (kHz to MHz): they can't follow; only holes at the edge of Wmax respond ⇒ C stays at Cmin.
  • Deep depletion: if the DC bias is swept very fast, no inversion layer has time to form; W keeps growing past Wmax and C falls below Cmin.
  • At flat band the capacitance is not Cox: the AC signal still moves charge to a small depth, the Debye length LD = √(εskT/(q²NA)). CDebye = εs/LD, and CFB = Cox in series with CDebye.
Worked: NA = 1016 cm-3, tox = 10 nm. Find LD, CDebye and CFB/Cox.
  1. LD = √(εsVT/(qNA)) = √(1.04×10-12 × 0.0259/(1.6×10-19 × 1016)) = 4.1×10-6 cm = 41 nm.
  2. CDebye = 1.04×10-12/4.1×10-6 = 2.53×10-7 F/cm²; Cox = 3.45×10-13/10-6 = 3.45×10-7 F/cm².
  3. CFB = 1/(1/3.45 + 1/2.53) × 10-7 = 1.46×10-7 ⇒ CFB/Cox ≈ 0.42.

13.16 The BJT, quantitatively (BJT1, BJT2)

  • Applications (Drive): switching in power electronics (block 1000 V or pass 10 A from a tiny control signal; DC–DC converters, inverters, motor drives, EV chargers), logic, memory, and amplifiers (power amplifiers, low-noise amplifiers at GHz).
  • Four steps in an npn: injection (E → B), transport and recombination in the base, collection (the reverse-biased CB field sweeps electrons into C), control: IC is set by VBE (injection) and base transport, not by VC.
  • Control mechanism: a small change in IB changes VBE a little, and because IE is exponential in VBE, IC changes a lot: amplification.
  • Base current IB = IEp (holes back-injected into the emitter) + IB,rec (holes lost to recombination in the base). IC = Inc + IBC,rev (pA, neglected).
Exact currents (n = electrons in the base, e = holes in the emitter; W = WBn)
Boundary conditions: nb(0) = (ni²/NAB)eqVBE/kT;   nb(W) ≈ 0
IE = [ qADnLnni²NAB coth(WLn) + qADeLeni²NDE ] (eqVBE/kT − 1)
IC = qADnLnni²NAB 1sinh(W/Ln) (eqVBE/kT − 1)
IB,rec ≈ qADn2Ln²ni²NAB W (eqVBE/kT − 1)
Figures of merit
γ ≈ 1 − NABDeWNDEDnLe    B = 1cosh(W/Ln) ≈ 1 − W²2Ln²    α = Bγ    β = α/(1 − α)
β limited by back-injection: β ≈ DnLeNDEDeWNAB    β limited by base recombination: β ≈ 2Ln²W²
Maximise β: raise NDE, lower NAB, shrink W (your set-A p.35 conclusions, now as formulas)
Worked: W = 1 μm, Ln = 10 μm, Le = 1 μm, Dn = 20, De = 2 cm²/s, NDE = 1019, NAB = 1017 cm-3. Find B, γ, α, β.
  1. B = 1/cosh(0.1) = 0.995 (recombination-limited β alone would be 2 × 100 = 200).
  2. γ = 1 − (1017 × 2 × 1)/(1019 × 20 × 1) = 1 − 0.001 = 0.999 (injection-limited β alone would be 1000).
  3. α = 0.995 × 0.999 = 0.994 ⇒ β = 0.994/0.006 ≈ 166. Base recombination is the main limit here; a thinner base would help most.
  • CB configuration: input IE, output IC, gain α < 1 (5 mA in, 4.9 mA out); output curves IC vs VCB, flat, stepping with IE. CE configuration: input IB (μA), output IC (mA), gain β (5 μA in, 0.5 to 5 mA out); curves IC vs VCE.
  • Early effect and its trade-off: the base is lightly doped, so the CB depletion region spreads into it as VCB rises, WBn falls and IC rises (sloped curves meeting at −VA; ideal VA = ∞). The Gummel number QG ≈ NABWBn (majority charge in the base) sets it: VA ∝ QG/CBC. A heavily doped base gives a big VA but lowers γ and β: the β vs VA trade-off. To raise VA without hurting β, make CBC small, i.e. a wide BC depletion region: the collector is the most lightly doped region.
Exam traps
  • Boltzmann formulas need EF at least 3kT from the band edge; otherwise the material is degenerate.
  • Donor factor 2, acceptor factor 4 in the ionisation formulas.
  • λcut-off = 1.24/Eg μm: a larger gap means a shorter wavelength.
  • Recombination current has η = 2 (eqV/2kT), diffusion η = 1.
  • Zener needs heavy doping on both sides; avalanche happens in lightly doped junctions and has the higher VBR.
  • High-frequency C–V stays at Cmin in inversion; low-frequency returns to Cox; deep depletion goes below Cmin.
  • BJT doping order: emitter heaviest, base medium/light, collector lightest.

CHAPTER 14Manufacturing: From Sand to a Working Chip

How the transistors of Chapters 9 to 12 are actually made: crystal growth, oxidation, doping by diffusion and implantation, lithography, thin films and epitaxy, and the complete NMOS process.

Drive: 3_Manufacturing notes (Crystal growth, Oxidation, Doping, Lithography, NMOS steps) Drive: slides M1 to M6
Explain like I'm 10

Making a chip is like printing a city with a very fancy stamp, many times over. First you need a perfect blank page: a slice of pure silicon crystal (made from sand). Then, layer by layer, you grow glass on it (oxidation), sprinkle special atoms into chosen spots (doping), draw the pattern for the next layer with light through a stencil (lithography), carve away what you don't want (etching) and paint on new layers like metal wires (deposition). Repeat 20 to 80 times and you have billions of transistors.

14.1 The big picture (M1, M2)

Design to chip: requirements → hardware description (HDL) → logic gates (synthesis) → layout (place and route) → cleanroom fabrication → testing and packaging.

Fabrication in one line: sand → polysilicon → ingot → slice → polish → [oxidise → photolithography (coat resist → spin → soft-bake → align and expose through the mask → develop) → etch → strip resist → dope] × many layers → metal interconnects (PVD/CVD) → passivation → dicing → packaging and bonding → test.

The five process categories (NMOS notes)Techniques
1. Wafer preparationCZ crystal growth (Bridgman for GaAs, float zone), sawing, lapping, etching, CMP polishing
2. Oxide formationdry or wet thermal oxidation
3. Patterninglithography (resist, mask, exposure, development) and etching
4. Dopingthermal diffusion, ion implantation
5. DepositionCVD, sputtering, vacuum evaporation

The steps are not strictly in this order; they repeat and interleave. Wafers are cleaned after almost every step.

14.2 The silicon crystal (M3)

  • Unit cells: simple cubic, body-centred cubic (BCC), face-centred cubic (FCC).
  • Silicon = the diamond lattice: two interpenetrating FCC lattices, one shifted from the other by a/4 along x, y and z. Each atom has 4 nearest neighbours (the 4 covalent bonds of Chapter 4).
  • Miller indices name crystal planes: take the plane's intercepts on x, y, z (in units of a), take reciprocals, and clear fractions to the smallest whole numbers. Wafers are cut along (100) or (111); (100) is used for MOS because it has the fewest interface traps. A direction is written in square brackets, e.g. [111].
  • Defects (all harmful): point defects (vacancy, interstitial), line defects (dislocations), area defects (stacking faults), volume defects (precipitates). Chapter 13's traps come from these.
Worked: a plane cuts the axes at x = 1, y = 2, z = ∞ (parallel to z). Find its Miller indices.

Intercepts (1, 2, ∞) → reciprocals (1, ½, 0) → multiply by 2 → (2 1 0). A plane cutting only x at 1 (parallel to y and z) is (1 0 0); one cutting all three at 1 is (1 1 1).

14.3 From sand to electronic-grade silicon (M3)

  1. Metallurgical-grade Si (MGS), 98 % pure: quartzite sand reduced with carbon in a submerged-electrode arc furnace at ~2000 °C: SiO2 + 2C → Si + 2CO. Impurities Al, Fe. (90 % of MGS goes to the steel industry.)
  2. Trichlorosilane: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2. SiHCl3 boils at 32 °C, so it is purified by fractional distillation.
  3. Electronic-grade Si (EGS): in a Siemens CVD reactor, 2SiHCl3 + 2H2 → 2Si + 6HCl deposits polysilicon nuggets with impurities at the parts-per-billion level (mainly B, P, C). EGS is about 99.999999999 % pure ("eleven nines").

14.4 Growing the single crystal: the Czochralski method

  • Invented in 1918; also called the "liquid–solid mono-component growth system". Essentially all IC wafers are CZ wafers. The other method is float zone (higher purity, no crucible); Bridgman is used for GaAs.
  • Parts: quartz (silica) crucible inside a graphite susceptor, graphite heater (RF induction or resistance), a chamber that is evacuated and then filled with argon, a crucible shaft rotating clockwise and a seed/pull shaft rotating anticlockwise holding a seed crystal of orientation ⟨100⟩ or ⟨111⟩.
  • Steps: load the crushed EGS ("the charge"), evacuate, fill with Ar, melt at about 1412 to 1417 °C (Si melts at 1414 °C), dip the seed, then pull slowly while rotating; silicon freezes onto the seed copying its orientation.
  • Control parameters: pull rate (a few mm/min; it sets the diameter: too slow and the seed melts back), melt temperature, and rotation rate (counter-rotation keeps the melt temperature uniform, no hot or cold spots).
  • Product: an ingot 8 to 16 inches (200 to 450 mm) in diameter, sliced into wafers 0.5 to 0.8 mm thick. Bigger wafers mean more chips per run.
  • Disadvantages: oxygen from the quartz crucible (≈ 1018 cm-3; a contaminant, but it also strengthens the wafer) and carbon from the graphite (≈ 1016 cm-3). The crucible cracks on cooling and can't be reused.
Wafer specifications (slide M2)
Diameter (mm)125150200300450
Thickness (mm)0.60–0.650.65–0.700.715–0.7350.755–0.7750.78–0.80
Primary flat (mm)40–4555–60none: a notch is used instead
Bow (μm)706030<30<30
Total thickness variation (μm)655010<10<10
Orientation(100) or (111), ±1°

Wafer preparation after the ingot: grind to diameter, mark the flat/notch, saw (wire saw), lap, etch away the damaged layer, and polish to a mirror finish by chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP).

14.5 Thermal oxidation

Silicon heated in O2 or steam grows its own glass, SiO2. The Si/SiO2 interface is one of the cleanest electrical interfaces known, which is a key reason silicon (not Ge or GaAs) dominates electronics. SiO2 has a band gap of ~9 eV and a high breakdown field.

Uses of the oxide

  • Gate dielectric (thin, highest quality)
  • Field / isolation oxide (thick; raises the parasitic Vth so no channel forms between neighbouring devices; LOCOS = local oxidation of silicon)
  • Mask against dopants (dopants diffuse far more slowly in SiO2)

Dry vs wet

DryWet
ReactionSi + O2 → SiO2Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2
Rateslowfast
Qualitydense, electrically superiorporous (OH groups), inferior
Used forgate oxidethick field oxide

Furnace procedure: load a quartz boat of 50 to 100 wafers into a quartz tube furnace (horizontal, or vertical for a smaller footprint and symmetric gas flow) slowly to avoid thermal shock; flush with inert gas; ramp to ~900 to 1200 °C; oxidise; ramp down; pull out slowly. The rate is exponential in temperature (Arrhenius), so temperature uniformity is critical.

Where the oxide grows: at the Si/SiO2 interface, not on top. The oxidant must diffuse through the oxide already there, then react with silicon. Silicon is consumed: the oxide is about 2.2 times the thickness of the silicon it eats, i.e. 44 % of the final oxide thickness is consumed silicon.

Deal–Grove model (M4)
F1 = hG(CG − CS) gas to surface    F2 = D(C* − Ci)/x0 diffusion through the oxide    F3 = ksCi reaction at the interface    steady state F1 = F2 = F3
x0² + A x0 = B(t + τ)    B = parabolic rate constant, B/A = linear rate constant, τ accounts for any initial oxide
Thin oxide (short t): x0 ≈ (B/A)(t + τ), linear, reaction-limited    Thick oxide (long t): x0² ≈ B(t + τ), parabolic, diffusion-limited (Ci ≈ 0)
Worked: with A = 0.165 μm, B = 0.0117 μm²/h and no initial oxide, how thick is the oxide after 2 h and after 10 h? How much silicon did the 2 h oxide consume?
  1. Solve the quadratic: x0 = [−A + √(A² + 4Bt)]/2.
  2. t = 2 h: √(0.0272 + 0.0936) = 0.348 ⇒ x0 = (0.348 − 0.165)/2 = 0.091 μm = 91 nm.
  3. t = 10 h: √(0.0272 + 0.468) = 0.704 ⇒ x0 = 0.27 μm. Five times the time gives only three times the oxide: growth slows as the oxide thickens.
  4. Si consumed at 2 h: 0.44 × 91 = 40 nm.
  • Oxide thickness by colour: light reflecting from the top and bottom of the film interferes. Destructive interference when 2noxd = (m + ½)λ removes some colours, so each thickness has a characteristic colour (a colour chart is used for quick checks, e.g. ~1000 Å looks violet).
  • Deal–Grove fails for very thin dry oxides (it underestimates the fast initial growth).
  • The thin-oxide limit: below ~2 nm electrons tunnel through the gate oxide (gate leakage). Modern chips replace SiO2 with high-k (hafnium-based) oxides, deposited by atomic-layer deposition (ALD) rather than grown: Cox = κε0/t, so a larger κ (SiO2 κ ≈ 3.9) gives the same Cox with a physically thicker, non-leaky film.

14.6 Doping by thermal diffusion

Why doping control matters (Drive): source/drain doping sets the parasitic resistance (lower R ⇒ more drive current); channel doping controls short-channel effects (higher doping suppresses punch-through and DIBL, Chapter 11); doping must be controlled vertically and laterally, which is hard in FinFETs and nanosheets.

  • The 1960s–80s method: wafers in a quartz furnace at 800 to 1000 °C (up to ~1200 °C) with a dopant source: POCl3 (phosphorus oxychloride) for n-type, boron sources for p-type. SiO2 windows define where dopant enters.
  • Only substitutional dopants are electrically active (sitting on a Si lattice site); interstitial ones are inactive.
  • Atomic mechanisms: vacancy-assisted (A + V ⇌ AV: the dopant hops into a neighbouring empty site) and interstitialcy / kick-out (A + I ⇌ AI).
  • The maximum concentration that dissolves is the solid solubility limit.
Fick's laws and Arrhenius
1st law: J = −D ∂C∂x    2nd law: ∂C∂t = D ∂²C∂x²    D = D0 exp(−Ea/kT)    diffusion length √(Dt)
(Fick's laws are accurate only at low concentrations; they fail at very high doping and during oxidation.)

Step 1: pre-deposition

Unlimited source at the surface ⇒ surface concentration fixed at Cs (the solubility limit).

C(x,t) = Cs erfc[x/(2√(Dt))]

Dose introduced: Q = 2Cs√(Dt/π) (∝ Cs√(Dt)).

Step 2: drive-in

Source removed; a fixed dose Q spreads deeper and the surface concentration falls.

C(x,t) = Q√(πDt) exp[−x²/(4Dt)] (Gaussian)

Junction depth where C = background CB: xj = 2√(Dt ln[Q/(CB√(πDt))]).

Worked: pre-deposition with Cs = 1020 cm-3, D = 10-14 cm²/s for 1 h; then drive-in with D = 5×10-13 cm²/s for 2 h into a substrate with CB = 1016 cm-3. Find the dose, the final surface concentration and the junction depth.
  1. Pre-dep: Dt = 10-14 × 3600 = 3.6×10-11 cm² (√(Dt) = 0.06 μm). Q = 2 × 1020 × √(3.6×10-11/π) = 6.8×1014 cm-2.
  2. Drive-in: Dt = 5×10-13 × 7200 = 3.6×10-9 cm²; √(πDt) = 1.06×10-4 cm. Surface C = Q/√(πDt) = 6.4×1018 cm-3 (it fell from 1020).
  3. xj = 2√(3.6×10-9 × ln(6.4×1018/1016)) = 2√(3.6×10-9 × 6.46) = 3.05×10-4 cm = 3.0 μm.

14.7 Ion implantation

The modern method (since the 1980s): dopant ions are accelerated and fired into the wafer. Precise, done at low temperature, and almost any film can be the mask (metal, thick SiO2, photoresist). The profile peaks below the surface.

The implanter, in beam order (Drive)
  1. Ion source / ioniser: electrons or a plasma ionise the dopant gas.
  2. Mass separator (analysing magnet): bends each ion by its mass/charge; only the wanted species passes the slit.
  3. Accelerator: sets the ion energy, and the energy sets the depth (keV to MeV).
  4. Scanning and focusing: X/Y electrostatic plates sweep the beam over the wafer.
  5. Neutral beam trap: neutral atoms can't be steered, so the beam is bent slightly and neutrals go straight into a trap.
  6. Faraday cup: collects the charge to measure the dose.

Typical parameters (M4): ions P, As, Sb, B, In, O; dose 1011 to 1018 cm-2; energy 1 to 400 keV; uniformity ±1 %; flux 1012 to 1014 cm-2s-1; depths 10 nm to 10 μm.

Implant profile
C(x) = Cp exp[ −(x − Rp)²2ΔRp² ]    Rp = projected range (mean depth), ΔRp = straggle (standard deviation)
Dose: Q = ∫C dx = √(2π) ΔRp Cp ⇒ Cp = Q/(√(2π)ΔRp) ≈ 0.4Q/ΔRp
  • Stopping: ions lose energy by nuclear stopping (collisions with Si nuclei: large deflections, they knock atoms out of place, crystal damage) and electronic stopping (drag by electrons: path almost unchanged, small energy loss, negligible damage). Light ions lose energy mostly electronically ⇒ deep; heavy ions mostly by nuclear collisions ⇒ shallow and damaging.
  • Annealing is mandatory: a heat treatment that repairs the lattice damage and moves implanted dopants from interstitial to substitutional sites (activation).
  • Mask thickness: must be enough that the concentration that gets through is below the substrate background: d ≥ Rp + ΔRp√(2 ln(Cp/CB)) (with the range values for the mask material).
Worked: a 1015 cm-2 implant with Rp = 0.3 μm, ΔRp = 0.07 μm. Find the peak concentration. How thick must a mask (assume the same Rp, ΔRp) be so that less than 1015 cm-3 gets through?
  1. Cp = 1015/(2.507 × 7×10-6 cm) = 5.7×1019 cm-3.
  2. ln(5.7×1019/1015) = 10.95 ⇒ √(2 × 10.95) = 4.68.
  3. d = 0.3 + 0.07 × 4.68 = 0.63 μm.
Feature (Drive comparison)Thermal diffusionIon implantation
Temperaturehigh (800 to 1200 °C)low (room temperature), but needs an anneal
