14.8 Photolithography

The cycle (repeated for every layer): deposit the film → coat with photoresist (spin-coat for uniform thickness) → soft-bake → align the mask and expose with UV (stepper/scanner) → develop → etch or implant through the openings → strip the resist. History (Drive): Moore's 1965 observation of doubling every ~2 years at similar cost; the first commercial monolithic IC (1961) had 4 transistors; Nvidia Hopper (2022) has 80 billion.

Positive resist

Exposed areas become soluble and wash away ⇒ the pattern left is the same as the mask. Higher resolution, better dimension (CD) control and alignment. The industry standard.

Negative resist

Exposed areas cross-link and become insoluble; the unexposed areas wash away ⇒ the pattern is the inverse of the mask. Better etch resistance, thicker films, but lower resolution (it swells in the developer).

Rayleigh resolution
R = k1 λNA    NA = n sin θ (numerical aperture of the lens; θ = half-angle of the light cone)    k1 = process factor (≥ 0.25)
Smaller features need: ↓λ, ↑NA, ↓k1
  • ↓λ: mercury lamps (g-line 436 nm, i-line 365 nm; many lines need filters; lamp ageing needs recalibration; chromatic aberration) → excimer lasers: DUV 248 nm (KrF), 193 nm (ArF) → EUV 13.5 nm for 7/5/3 nm nodes. EUV light is made by hitting tin droplets (50,000 per second) with two infrared laser pulses (one flattens the droplet, the next vaporises it into a plasma). EUV is absorbed by everything, including glass and air, so it needs reflective multilayer mirrors in vacuum instead of lenses.
  • ↑NA: large aspheric lenses (beyond ~0.8), then immersion lithography: water between the lens and wafer raises n, so NA up to ~1.35. 193 nm immersion is the industry workhorse.
  • ↓k1: computational lithography and optical proximity correction (OPC) (pre-distort the mask so the printed shape comes out right; sub-resolution assist features; free-form OPC), off-axis (annular, dipole) illumination with programmable micromirror illuminators (FlexRay), phase-shift masks, and multiple patterning (split one dense layer into two or more exposures).
Worked: find the resolution of (a) 193 nm immersion with NA = 1.35 and k1 = 0.3, (b) EUV with NA = 0.33 and k1 = 0.4.

(a) R = 0.3 × 193/1.35 = 43 nm. (b) R = 0.4 × 13.5/0.33 = 16 nm. EUV gains mostly from the 14× shorter wavelength, even though its NA is lower.

14.9 Thin films and epitaxy (M6)

Films on a chip are dielectrics (SiO2, Si3N4), semiconductors (polysilicon, epitaxial Si), metals and polymers.

CVD (chemical vapour deposition)PVD (physical vapour deposition)
Howreactant gases react on the hot wafer surface and leave a solid filma solid source is vaporised and condenses on the wafer
TypesAPCVD (atmospheric), LPCVD (low pressure), PECVD (plasma-enhanced), VPEevaporation (thermal, e-beam), sputtering (DC, RF)
Coverageexcellent step coverage, conformalline-of-sight, shadowing
Typical filmsdielectrics, epitaxial and polysiliconmetals, silicides, contacts

Epitaxy ("epi" = upon, "taxis" = ordered): growing a single-crystal film that continues the substrate's crystal.

  • Homoepitaxy: same material (Si on Si), to get a purer layer with different doping. Heteroepitaxy: different material (e.g. AlGaAs on GaAs), for band engineering.
  • Why: a high-purity device layer; growth at a lower temperature than diffusion, so doping steps stay sharp; free choice of thickness and doping; heterojunction bipolar transistors (Kroemer, Nobel Prize 2000); HEMTs with a 2-D electron gas; SOI, silicon-on-sapphire, SiC; a lightly doped p layer on a p⁺ substrate to reduce latch-up in CMOS; buried layers in bipolar ICs.
  • Types: VPE (vapour phase: a CVD process at 800 to 1100 °C), LPE (liquid phase, from a melt), MBE (molecular beam epitaxy: atomic beams in ultra-high vacuum ~10-8 Pa, monolayer control).
  • The seven CVD steps: (1) gas transport to the reactor, (2) diffusion across the boundary layer, (3) adsorption on the surface, (4) surface reaction, (5) desorption of by-products, (6) diffusion of by-products back across the boundary layer, (7) removal. Steps 2 to 5 set the growth rate; 3 to 5 are the surface reaction.
  • Reactors: horizontal atmospheric cold-wall (RF-heated graphite susceptor; SiCl4 + 2H2 → Si + 4HCl), low-pressure hot-wall (polysilicon, SiO2), pancake, barrel.
  • Si sources and temperatures: SiCl4 ~1200 °C, SiHCl3 ~1150 °C, SiH2Cl2 ~1100 °C, SiH4 ~1050 °C. The reverse reaction SiCl4 + Si ⇌ 2SiCl2 etches: growth rate vs SiCl4 mole fraction peaks near y ≈ 0.1 and becomes etching above y ≈ 0.27.

14.10 Putting it together: the metal-gate NMOS process

The 20 steps of slide M2 (four masks)
  1. Start with a p-type substrate.
  2. Grow a thick SiO2 layer (900 to 1200 °C).
  3. Coat with positive photoresist.
  4. Mask 1 (source/drain windows): lithography.
  5. UV changes the exposed resist.
  6. Developer removes the exposed resist.
  7. Etch the uncovered SiO2 with HF (hydrofluoric acid).
  8. Strip the remaining resist with piranha (H2SO4 : H2O2 ≈ 3 : 1).
  9. Form the n⁺ source and drain by diffusion or implantation.
  10. Cover the wafer with SiO2 again.
  11. Coat with positive resist.
  12. Mask 2: lithography for the gate region (and contact openings).
  13. Expose.
  14. Develop/remove the exposed resist.
  15. Etch the SiO2 over the gate region.
  16. Grow the thin gate oxide.
  17. Mask 3: remove the thin oxide over the source/drain contacts, keeping it over the gate.
  18. Deposit metal (Al) over everything.
  19. Mask 4: pattern the Al to separate source, gate and drain.
  20. Passivation / overglassing to protect the chip, leaving the bond pads open.

A CMOS process adds an n-well (Chapter 10 figure) for the pMOS, p⁺ implants for its source/drain, field-oxide isolation and, in modern processes, a polysilicon (or metal) self-aligned gate, followed by many layers of copper interconnect.

Exam traps
  • Oxide grows at the Si/SiO2 interface, consuming 0.44 of its thickness in Si; it does not just sit on top.
  • Thin oxide: linear, reaction-limited. Thick oxide: parabolic, diffusion-limited.
  • Pre-deposition = constant surface concentration (erfc). Drive-in = constant dose (Gaussian).
  • Implant: light ion deeper; energy sets depth; always needs an anneal.
  • Positive resist: exposed part dissolves, pattern = mask. Negative: the opposite.
  • R = k1λ/NA: immersion raises NA; EUV lowers λ.
  • CZ: crucible clockwise, seed anticlockwise; pull rate sets the diameter; O from the crucible, C from the susceptor.

CHAPTER 15Circuit Simulation: SPICE, LTspice and MOSFET Models

Before spending millions on masks, every chip is simulated. This chapter covers what SPICE is, how it solves a circuit, the MOSFET model levels, the netlist and analyses, and the lab experiment from class.

Drive: 4_LTSpice (Class Notes, Notes_MOSFET_SPICE_Models, slides LT1 to LT5)
Explain like I'm 10

Building a real chip is like baking a giant cake that takes three months and costs a fortune, and you can't fix it once it's baked. So first you bake it in a video game. SPICE is that game: you describe the circuit as a list of parts and connections, and it calculates every voltage and current. If the game cake comes out flat, you change the recipe for free.

15.1 What SPICE is

  • SPICE = Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis, from UC Berkeley, 1973 (open source). Versions: 1973 SPICE1 (FORTRAN), 1975 SPICE2, 1981 SPICE 2G.6, 1985 SPICE3 (rewritten in C).
  • Why simulate: fabrication is expensive and irreversible, so verify first. Commercial EDA vendors: Cadence, Synopsys, Mentor Graphics (Siemens), Tanner. Free tools: LTspice (Analog Devices, download from analog.com), PSpice Lite (Cadence OrCAD; limited to 64 nodes, 10 transistors, 2 op-amps, 65 digital primitives).
  • A general-purpose circuit simulator for non-linear DC, non-linear transient and linear AC analysis. It writes the circuit equations with KCL and KVL using modified nodal analysis and solves non-linear devices iteratively with Newton's method (linearise, solve, repeat until the answer stops changing: "convergence").
  • A device model is an analytical expression built from theory and measurement. Two kinds: device (primitive) models (.model) and subcircuit models (.subckt, a block built from other parts). A model reproduces only the behaviour its equations contain, not every quirk on a datasheet.

15.2 The netlist: instance letters and analyses

LetterElementPins (order)
MMOSFETD G S B (4 pins)
QBJTC B E
DdiodeA K (anode, cathode)
R, C, Lresistor, capacitor, inductor2 pins
V, Ivoltage / current source+ −
Evoltage-controlled voltage source (VCVS)4 pins
Gvoltage-controlled current source (VCCS)4 pins

Analyses

  • .op / .dc: static operating point and DC sweeps (datasheet DC curves)
  • .ac: small-signal frequency response (gain, phase, capacitance effects)
  • .tran: time response, like an oscilloscope
  • Monte Carlo: random component variation, run many times to see the spread

LTspice survival kit (LT3)

  • F5 or Ctrl-X: delete; F7: move; F8: drag (keeps wires attached)
  • Ctrl-R: rotate; Ctrl-E: mirror
  • Right-click a part to enter its value or model
  • .include a model file; put dot-commands on the schematic as "SPICE directives"

15.3 The SPICE diode model (LT4)

  • Equivalent circuit: the ideal exponential diode current IF, a junction capacitance Cj and a series resistance RS.
  • Cj = Cj0/(1 − V/Vbi)M (M = grading coefficient; ½ for an abrupt junction, matching Chapter 13).
  • N = emission coefficient = the ideality factor η of Chapter 13: I = IS(eV/NVT − 1).
  • Class example: .model 1mA_diode D (Is=100pA n=1.679) with .DC VD 0V 800mV 10mV: the simulator used as a curve tracer.
  • A DC restorer (clamper) example: a PULSE(−3 7 …) source, 1 μF and a 1N4148, analysed with .TRAN 100u 10m.

15.4 The MOSFET model in SPICE

  • ID = f(constants μn, μp, Cox, Vth; variables VGS, VDS), placed between the internal drain D′ and source S′.
  • RD, RS: series resistances of the drain and source regions.
  • Cgd, Cgs, Cgb: gate (MOS) capacitances. In Level 1 they follow the Meyer model, different in triode and saturation and smoothed at the boundary.
  • D–B and S–B diodes (always reverse-biased in normal use) with their depletion capacitances Cdb, Csb.
  • Level 1 in SPICE form: ID = (K′/2)(W/Leff)[2(VGS − VT)VDS − VDS²](1 + λVDS), with K′ = μCox and Leff = L − 2LD. This is exactly your triode formula ① with CLM (Chapter 11). Effective sizes use parameters such as LD, WD, XL, XW, LMLT, WMLT.
ModelBasisParametersGood forLimitations
Level 1 (Shichman–Hodges)square law, GCA~7 (K′/μ, Cox/tox, VT, λ, γ, φ, W, L)hand calculation, fast large digital simulationsno sub-threshold, no SCEs; accurate only for L ≳ 4 μm (some notes: ≳ 0.8 μm); predicts saturation output resistance poorly
Level 2physics-basedmoreadds SCEs, sub-threshold, bulk-charge effects, field-dependent mobilitycomplex, slow, convergence problems
Level 3semi-empirical (fitted to measurements)moresame accuracy as Level 2 with better convergenceloses accuracy at sub-micron
BSIM (Level 4, 7/49/54…; Berkeley Short-channel IGFET Model)physical + fitted> 100deep sub-micron; industry standard; needed below ~0.8 μmnot for hand analysis
EKV (Enz–Krummenacher–Vittoz)single continuous equationcompactweak to strong inversion with no jump in derivatives; low-power analog/RF

Model generations (LT5): 1st (Levels 1, 2, 3); 2nd (BSIM, BSIM2, HSPICE Level 28); 3rd (BSIM3 / Level 7/49, adding stress, sub-threshold, noise, gate tunnelling and temperature effects). The second-order effects that need BSIM3 below 0.8 μm (class notes): short-channel threshold shift, sub-threshold conduction, velocity saturation, charge-controlled capacitances.

  • Model file = a text file of technology parameters (.model or .lib), loaded with .include. PTM (Predictive Technology Models) provide files for 180 nm down to 90/65/45/32/22/16 nm. All devices in one circuit must use the same technology.
  • Rule of thumb from the Drive: hand calculations use Level 1; EDA sign-off uses BSIM.

15.5 Experiment 6: nMOS characteristics and the inverter in LTspice

The lab exactly as in your class notes
  1. Place an nmos4 symbol (4 terminals). Set L = 0.18 μm (180 nm), W = 10 μm; .include the 180 nm model file.
  2. Source V2 on the drain (VDS), V1 on the gate (VGS); source and body grounded.
  3. Nested DC sweep: VDS from 0 to 1.8 V in 0.01 V steps, for VGS = 0 to 1.8 V in 0.3 V steps:
    .dc V2 0 1.8 0.01 V1 0 1.8 0.3
  4. Plot ID (Id(M1)): a family of output curves like Chapter 11's figure.
  5. Transfer curve: sweep VGS at fixed VDS and find gm = ∂ID/∂VGS (LTspice can plot d(Id(M1))).
  6. Build the CMOS inverter (add a pmos4 with its source and body at VDD = 1.8 V), sweep Vin with .dc to get the VTC (Chapter 12), then apply a PULSE input with .tran to see the transient (propagation delay).
Practice: write the SPICE lines for (a) an nMOS M1 with drain node d, gate g, source and body at 0, model NMOS180, W = 10 μm, L = 0.18 μm; (b) a sweep of VDS 0 to 1.8 V for VGS = 0.6, 1.2, 1.8 V; (c) a 10 ns transient.

(a) M1 d g 0 0 NMOS180 W=10u L=0.18u (pin order D G S B).

(b) VDS d 0 0, VGS g 0 0, .dc VDS 0 1.8 0.01 VGS 0.6 1.8 0.6.

(c) .tran 10n (or .tran 0.01n 10n to set the step), with a source such as VIN in 0 PULSE(0 1.8 1n 50p 50p 2n 4n).

Exam traps
  • MOSFET pin order is D G S B; BJT is C B E.
  • SPICE solves non-linear circuits with Newton's method; non-convergence means the iteration did not settle.
  • Level 1 = Shichman–Hodges square law: no sub-threshold current, no short-channel effects.
  • "N" in a diode model is the emission coefficient (ideality factor), not a doping.

CHAPTER 16Semiconductor Memories

How billions of bits are stored on a chip: what defines a good memory, ROM vs RAM, how the array is organised and addressed, the NOR ROM from your board notes, and the SRAM and DRAM cells.

Drive: board notes 1112-1600; Semiconductor_Memories_Lecture_Notes
Explain like I'm 10

A memory chip is a giant apartment block where each flat holds one bit (a 0 or a 1). To visit a flat you need its floor number (the row, picked by the word line) and its door number (the column, reached through the bit line). A ROM is a block where the furniture was cemented in when it was built: you can look, not change. A RAM lets you move furniture any time, but if the power goes off (the lights go out) everyone forgets where everything was.

16.1 What a memory is and how it is judged

  • Memory = an electronic circuit that can store data. Bit = the smallest unit of data that can be stored. The basic building block is a 1-bit cell, replicated in an array. Modern memories are built from MOSFETs for density, low power and speed.
Performance metric (board + typed notes)Meaning
Area efficiency / storage densitybits per unit area (tape and floppy were huge; an SD card holds up to 512 GB on a fingernail)
Cost per bitfewer transistors per cell ⇒ cheaper bits
Access timetime to read or write a chosen location; it defines the speed of the memory
Power: staticstandby power when nothing switches (leakage, refresh)
Power: dynamicpower spent when nodes switch 0 ↔ 1
Data retention timehow long stored data stays valid

The board sums it up as area, speed, power: the same three-way trade-off as all of VLSI.

Testing (typed notes: design for testability)

After fabrication every chip must be tested against expected outputs. With thousands of inputs, testing every combination is impossible (input-vector explosion: n inputs give 2n combinations), so tests use random samples / chosen test patterns and fault models (what physical defects can occur and what wrong outputs they would cause). Designing the chip so it is easy to test is design for testability (DFT).

16.2 Classification

The board classifies memories by (i) type of data storage and (ii) type of data access:

Read-only memory (ROM)

  1. Only retrieval of data (mostly reads)
  2. Data stored at the time of fabrication or programming
  3. Non-volatile: keeps data with the power off

Mask-programmed ROM (fixed by a mask during manufacture) · PROM (programmable once by the user in the field) · EPROM (erasable, with UV light, and re-writable many times) · EEPROM (electrically erasable) · Flash (high-density electrically erasable; SD cards, SSDs). Programmable kinds have limited write endurance and writes are much slower than reads.

Read/write memory (RAM)

  1. Allows re-writing of data
  2. Volatile: loses data when power is removed
  3. Random access: no need to go through locations in sequence; fast reads and writes

SRAM (static RAM: cross-coupled transistors hold the bit as long as power is on) · DRAM (dynamic RAM: the bit is charge on a capacitor that leaks and must be periodically refreshed).

16.3 Memory organisation

  • Memory cell: each stores one bit. Cells are placed in an array (the memory core) surrounded by peripherals (decoders, sense amplifiers, drivers, timing).
  • Row decoder: N address bits A1…AN select one of 2N word lines (an N-input decoder has 2N outputs).
  • Word lines = horizontal lines connecting all the cells in a row. Bit lines = vertical lines used to read or write a specific cell.
  • Column decoder: M address bits pick one of 2M bit lines.
  • Storage capacity = 2N × 2M bits (the board writes 2m × 2n).
  • To read or write a cell, both its word line and its bit line must be activated.
Worked: a 1 Mbit memory is organised as a square array. How many rows and columns, and how many address bits go to each decoder? What is the total address width?

1 Mbit = 220 bits. Square: 210 × 210 = 1024 rows × 1024 columns. Row decoder N = 10 bits, column decoder M = 10 bits, total 20 address bits. Why square? It keeps the word and bit lines (and so their capacitance and delay) as short as possible.

16.4 ROM circuits: the 4 × 4 NOR ROM (your board)

  1. Each column (bit line C1 to C4) has a pMOS pull-up with its gate grounded (always ON): the pseudo-nMOS load of Chapter 12. With no row selected, every column sits at 1.
  2. Rows R1 to R4 (word lines, driven by the row decoder) go to the gates of the nMOS cells. Exactly one row is 1 at a time.
  3. At a crossing (Ri, Cj): an nMOS present ⇒ when Ri = 1 it turns on and pulls Cj to 0. No transistor ⇒ Cj stays 1.
  4. Each column is a NOR of the rows that have transistors on it (any of them high ⇒ 0), hence "NOR ROM".
  5. The data is programmed by placing or omitting transistors at fabrication (a mask-programmed ROM).
Selected rowTransistors onC1C2C3C4Stored word
R1 = 1C1, C301010101 (board ✓)
R2 = 1C1, C200110011
R3 = 1C2, C310011001 (board ✓)
R4 = 1C1, C401100110
Practice: design a 4 × 4 NOR ROM storing R1 = 1010, R2 = 0111, R3 = 1111, R4 = 0000. Where do the transistors go? How many are needed?

Put a transistor wherever the stored bit is 0. R1 = 1010 ⇒ C2, C4. R2 = 0111 ⇒ C1. R3 = 1111 ⇒ none. R4 = 0000 ⇒ C1, C2, C3, C4. Total 7 nMOS + 4 pull-ups.

Beyond your notes: NAND ROM, and the programmable ROMs

In a NAND ROM the cell transistors of a column are in series; unselected rows are held high (all on) and the selected row goes low. It is denser (no ground contact per cell) but slower. EPROM/EEPROM/Flash cells are MOSFETs with an extra floating gate buried in the oxide: trapping electrons on it raises Vth, so the cell no longer turns on when its word line rises, storing a different bit. EPROMs are erased by UV light; EEPROM and Flash are erased electrically by tunnelling (Flash erases a whole block at once, which makes it dense and cheap).

16.5 RAM cells: SRAM and DRAM

Beyond your notes: how the cells work (the typed notes name them; standard detail added)

SRAM (6T)

  • Two CMOS inverters connected in a loop (cross-coupled): Q feeds the second inverter, which feeds back Q̄ into the first. The loop has two stable states, so it holds a bit as long as power is on with no refresh.
  • Two nMOS access transistors connect Q and Q̄ to the bit lines BL and BL̄ when the word line WL = 1.
  • Read: precharge BL and BL̄ high, raise WL; the side storing 0 pulls its bit line down a little; a sense amplifier detects the difference.
  • Write: drive BL/BL̄ to the new value strongly and raise WL; the drivers overpower the inverters.
  • Fast, no refresh, but 6 transistors per bit ⇒ large and expensive. Used for caches and registers.

DRAM (1T1C)

  • One access transistor and one storage capacitor CS: charged = 1, empty = 0.
  • Write: raise WL and drive BL to VDD or 0.
  • Read: precharge BL to VDD/2, raise WL; CS shares its charge with the much bigger bit-line capacitance CBL, moving BL slightly up or down: ΔV = (VS − VDD/2)·CS/(CS + CBL). Reading destroys the stored charge, so the sense amplifier writes it back.
  • Charge leaks through the transistor and junction (Chapter 13 generation current), so every cell is refreshed every few milliseconds.
  • Only 1 transistor per bit ⇒ the densest, cheapest RAM. Used for main memory.
Worked: a DRAM cell has CS = 25 fF, the bit line CBL = 250 fF, VDD = 1.2 V, precharge 0.6 V. What bit-line swing does the sense amplifier see when reading a 1 (cell at 1.2 V) and a 0?

ΔV = (VS − 0.6) × 25/(25 + 250) = (VS − 0.6) × 0.0909. Reading a 1: (0.6) × 0.0909 = +55 mV. Reading a 0: (−0.6) × 0.0909 = −55 mV. These tiny signals are why DRAM needs sensitive sense amplifiers, and why CS can't be shrunk freely.

Mask ROMFlashSRAMDRAM
Volatile?nonoyesyes
Cell0 or 1 transistor1 floating-gate transistor6 transistors1 transistor + 1 capacitor
Writeat fabricationslow, limited cyclesfastfast
Refreshnononoyes
Density / cost per bitvery high / lowvery high / lowestlow / highhigh / low
Typical usefixed firmware, look-up tablesSSDs, SD cards, phonesCPU cachesmain memory
Exam traps
  • Word lines are rows (horizontal), bit lines are columns (vertical).
  • N address bits select 2N lines; capacity = 2N × 2M bits.
  • In a NOR ROM a transistor at a crossing stores a 0; no transistor stores a 1.
  • ROM is non-volatile; RAM is volatile. "Random access" means any location in the same time, not "random data".
  • SRAM: no refresh, 6T, fast, big. DRAM: refresh, 1T1C, dense, destructive read.

Constant-field scaling by S: dimensions, V ÷S; I ÷S; delay ÷S; power ÷S²; power density 1. Constant-voltage: I ×S; delay ÷S²; power ×S; density ×S³

CMOS inverter and gates (Ch. 12)

tpHL = 0.69RnCL   tpLH = 0.69RpCL   tp = average
VM = [Vtn + r(VDD − |Vtp|)]/(1 + r), r = √(kp/kn)   symmetric when (W/L)p = (μn/μp)(W/L)n
NML = VIL − VOL, NMH = VOH − VIH (slope −1 points)   matched: VIL = (3VDD + 2Vt)/8, VIH = (5VDD − 2Vt)/8
Pdyn = αCLVDD²f   energy per 0→1→0 cycle = CLVDD²   Av = dVout/dVin
PDN: AND = series, OR = parallel; PUN = dual; output inverted; 2N transistors (pseudo-nMOS N + 1)

Unit I and MOS extras (Ch. 13)

n = Nce−(Ec − EF)/kT, p = Nve−(EF − Ev)/kT (valid if ≥ 3kT from the edge)   ni = √(NcNv)e−Eg/2kT
ND+/ND = 1/(1 + 2e(EF − ED)/kT)   NA−/NA = 1/(1 + 4e(EA − EF)/kT)   μ = qτ/m*   τ = 1/(σvthNt)
λc(μm) = 1.24/Eg(eV)   ∂n/∂t = (1/q)∂Jn/∂x + GL − U   L = √(Dτ)   Δn = GLτ   Δn(t) = GLτe−t/τ
Emax = qNDWn/εs = 2Vbi/W   Jrec = (qniW/2τ)eqV/2kT   Jgen = qniW/2τ   J ∝ eqV/ηkT
VBR = ½WFcrit = εsFcrit²/(2qN)   M = 1/(1 − ∫α dx)   1/C² = 2(Vbi − V)/(qεsND)   VOC = VTln(Iph/I0 + 1)
φF = VTln(NA/ni); strong inversion ψs = 2φF   LD = √(εskT/q²NA), CFB = Cox in series with CDebye
BJT: γ ≈ 1 − NABDeW/(NDEDnLe)   B = 1/cosh(W/Ln) ≈ 1 − W²/2Ln²   β ≈ 2Ln²/W² or DnLeNDE/(DeWNAB)   QG = NABW

Manufacturing (Ch. 14)

EGS: SiO2 + 2C → Si + 2CO; Si + 3HCl → SiHCl3 + H2; 2SiHCl3 + 2H2 → 2Si + 6HCl
Dry: Si + O2 → SiO2; wet: Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2   Si consumed = 0.44 xox   Deal–Grove x² + Ax = B(t + τ)
Fick: J = −D∂C/∂x, ∂C/∂t = D∂²C/∂x², D = D0e−Ea/kT   pre-dep Cserfc(x/2√Dt), Q = 2Cs√(Dt/π)   drive-in (Q/√(πDt))e−x²/4Dt
Implant: C(x) = Cpe−(x − Rp)²/2ΔRp², Q = √(2π)ΔRpCp   Lithography: R = k1λ/NA, NA = n sinθ   oxide colour 2noxd = (m + ½)λ

CHAPTER 18Practice Bank with Full Solutions

Try each question on paper first, then open the answer. Ordered like the course: A to F for Chapters 1 to 10, H to M for Chapters 11 to 16. The last group (N) tests understanding in words.

How to use it

Do parts A to M once, then redo only the ones you missed two days later. When a question looks new, it is almost always one of your class questions with different numbers.

A. Bands and Fermi statistics

A1. Compute the thermal energy kBT at 400 K in eV and meV.

kBT = 8.617×10-5 × 400 = 0.03447 eV = 34.5 meV. (Scales linearly with T: 300 → 25.85, 400 → 34.5.)

A2. For N carbon atoms, state the number of outer states and electrons, and how many states are in the valence band and conduction band.

Outer states 8N (2N from 2s, 6N from 2p). Outer electrons 4N. After band formation: VB = 4N states (all filled with 4N electrons), CB = 4N states (empty at 0 K).

A3. Two semiconductors have E–k curves near the band edge: A with d²E/dk² = 2×10-38 J·m², B with 0.5×10-38. Which has higher mobility (same τ)? Find m*A/m*B.

m* = ħ²/(d²E/dk²), so m* is inversely proportional to the curvature. m*A/m*B = 0.5/2 = 0.25. A is lighter, so with equal τ, μ = qτ/m* is 4× higher for A, and A has the higher current density.

A4. At 300 K, what is the probability that a state 0.05 eV above EF is occupied? What about 0.05 eV below?

Above: f = 1/(1 + e0.05/0.02585) = 1/(1 + 6.92) = 0.126. Below: 1 − 0.126 = 0.874. (Symmetry: f(EF + Δ) + f(EF − Δ) = 1.)

A5. Explain why GaAs is used for LEDs but Si is not.

GaAs is a direct-gap semiconductor: an electron and hole at the same k can recombine and release a photon directly. Si is indirect: recombination also needs a phonon to conserve momentum, which is a rare three-body event, so energy mostly goes to heat.

B. Carrier concentration

B1. Si (ni = 1.5×1010) is doped with ND = 2×1015 cm-3. Find n and p. What type is it?

n ≈ ND = 2×1015; p = ni²/n = 2.25×1020/2×1015 = 1.125×105 cm-3. n ≫ p ⇒ n-type.

B2. p-type Si with NA = 5×1016. Find p, n and the position of EF relative to Ei.

p ≈ 5×1016; n = 2.25×1020/5×1016 = 4500 cm-3. EF − Ei = −kBT ln(p/ni) = −0.0259 × ln(3.33×106) = −0.389 eV: 0.39 eV below mid-gap, i.e. only about 0.17 eV above Ev for a 1.12 eV gap.

B3. A Si sample has ND = 8×1015 and NA = 3×1015. Which type is it and what are n, p?

Net ND − NA = 5×1015 ≫ ni, so n-type, n ≈ 5×1015, p = 2.25×1020/5×1015 = 4.5×104.

B4. Why does n·p stay equal to ni² even after heavy doping, and what happens to the minority-carrier count?

Generation (thermal) and recombination (electron meets hole) reach a balance where the rates are proportional to n·p. Extra electrons from donors increase the recombination rate of holes, so holes fall until np returns to the equilibrium value ni². Minority carriers decrease by the same factor by which majority carriers increase.

C. Transport

C1. n-type Si with ND = 1015 cm-3, μn = 1350. Find σ and ρ. Then find the drift velocity and current density for 𝓔 = 100 V/cm.

σ = qNDμn = 1.6×10-19 × 1015 × 1350 = 0.216 S/cm, ρ = 4.63 Ω·cm. Vd = 1350 × 100 = 1.35×105 cm/s (still ≪ thermal speed ≈ 107 cm/s). J = σ𝓔 = 0.216 × 100 = 21.6 A/cm².

C2. Find the mean free time τ if μn = 1350 cm²/V·s and m* = 0.26 m0.

μ = 0.135 m²/V·s in SI. τ = μ m*/q = 0.135 × 0.26 × 9.11×10-31 / 1.6×10-19 = 2.0×10-13 s = 0.2 ps. With a thermal speed of 107 cm/s, the mean free path is about 20 nm.

C3. Using Einstein's relation find Dp for μp = 450 at 300 K, and Lp if τp = 1 μs.

Dp = μpVT = 450 × 0.0259 = 11.7 cm²/s. Lp = √(Dpτp) = √(11.7 × 10-6) = 3.4×10-3 cm = 34 μm.

C4. An electron density in Si varies linearly from 1016 cm-3 at x = 0 to 1015 cm-3 at x = 1 μm. With Dn = 30 cm²/s find the diffusion current density and its direction.

dn/dx = (1015 − 1016)/10-4 cm = −9×1019 cm-4. Jn = qDndn/dx = 1.6×10-19 × 30 × (−9×1019) = −432 A/cm². Electrons diffuse to +x (down the gradient), so the current flows toward −x.

C5. Light generates carriers in n-type Si (ND = 1015) at G = 1019 cm-3s-1. If the minority lifetime is 1 μs, find the steady-state excess carriers and the change in minority concentration.

In steady state generation = recombination: G = U = Δp/τ ⇒ Δp = Gτ = 1019 × 10-6 = 1013 cm-3. Equilibrium minority p0 = 2.25×105, so p ≈ 1013, an increase of about 4×107 times. The majority electrons change by only 1013/1015 = 1 %. This is why photodetectors respond to minority carriers.

C6. Sketch and explain why mobility peaks at an intermediate temperature in a moderately doped Si sample.

Low T: slow carriers are strongly scattered by ionised impurities, μII is small and rising with T. High T: lattice vibrations (phonons) scatter more, μph falls with T. Since 1/μ = 1/μph + 1/μII, the smaller one dominates at each end, giving a hill with a maximum where the two are comparable. More doping raises the low-T side (more impurity scattering) and lowers the peak.

D. p–n junction

D1. Find V0, W, xn, xp for NA = ND = 1016 cm-3, ni = 1.5×1010, T = 300 K.

V0 = 0.0259 ln(1032/2.25×1020) = 0.0259 × 26.82 = 0.695 V. W = √[(2 × 1.04×10-12/1.6×10-19)(2×10-16)(0.695)] = √(1.81×10-9) = 4.25×10-5 cm = 0.425 μm. Symmetric doping ⇒ xn = xp = 0.212 μm.

D2. In a junction with NA = 4×1016 and ND = 1016, which side has the wider depletion layer, and by what factor?

xn/xp = NA/ND = 4. The n-side (lightly doped) has the wider layer, four times the p-side layer. With W = 1 μm, xn = 0.8 μm and xp = 0.2 μm.

D3. A silicon diode has V0 = 0.7 V and W = 0.4 μm at zero bias. What is W at VR = 4.3 V?

W ∝ √(V0 + VR). W = 0.4 × √(5.0/0.7) = 0.4 × 2.673 = 1.07 μm.

D4. A diode carries 1 mA at 0.65 V. What voltage is needed for 10 mA? For 100 μA? (T = 300 K)

I ∝ eV/VT, so ΔV = VT ln(I2/I1). ×10 current: ΔV = 0.0259 × 2.303 = 59.6 mV. So 10 mA at 0.710 V, and 100 μA at 0.590 V (about 60 mV per decade).

D5. Why does an ideal reverse-biased diode carry −Is regardless of the voltage, and why does a real one show a slow rise before breakdown?

In reverse bias the barrier is so high that no majority carriers cross; the only current is the drift of the few thermally generated minority carriers near the junction, whose supply is fixed by temperature (not by voltage), so it saturates at Is. In real diodes, thermal generation inside the growing depletion region adds a component that increases with W (and therefore with VR), plus surface leakage.

D6. Classify the breakdown type: (a) VBR = 3.3 V heavily doped junction; (b) VBR = 40 V lightly doped junction.

(a) Zener (tunnelling; high doping ⇒ very thin depletion region ⇒ huge field at low voltage; VBR < 5 V). (b) Avalanche (impact ionisation; wide, lightly doped region ⇒ carriers accelerate over long distance; VBR > 8 V).

D7. For the diode of Section 7.9, what is the hole-injection fraction if ND is raised to 1018 and NA lowered to 1016?

The ratio Ip/In = (Dp/Dn)(Ln/Lp)(NA/ND) = (10/18)(10/5)(1016/1018) = 0.556 × 2 × 0.01 = 0.0111. So the electron current now dominates: hole fraction = 0.0111/1.0111 = 1.1 %. The majority carrier of the heavily-doped side always carries most of the current.

E. BJT

E1. An npn BJT has IE = 5 mA and α = 0.99. Find IC, IB, β.

IC = αIE = 4.95 mA. IB = IE − IC = 0.05 mA. β = 4.95/0.05 = 99 (α/(1−α) = 0.99/0.01 ✔).

E2. A BJT with β = 150 has IB = 50 μA. Find IC, IE, α.

IC = 150 × 50 μA = 7.5 mA; IE = 7.55 mA; α = 150/151 = 0.9934.

E3. B = 0.99 and γE = 0.98. Find α and β. Which one would you improve first to increase β, and why?

α = 0.99 × 0.98 = 0.9702; β = 0.9702/0.0298 = 32.6. Either factor matters equally at first order; but the emitter injection efficiency is usually easiest to fix (increase the emitter/base doping ratio), while B improves with a thinner base. Making γE = 0.995 would give α = 0.985 and β ≈ 66: doubling the gain.

E4. State the bias on EBJ and CBJ for (a) an amplifier, (b) a closed switch, (c) an open switch.

(a) Active: EBJ forward, CBJ reverse. (b) Saturation: both forward. (c) Cut-off: both reverse.

E5. A BJT has VA = 80 V and IC = 2 mA. Find the output resistance and the change in IC if VCE increases by 8 V.

ro ≈ VA/IC = 80/2 mA = 40 kΩ. ΔIC = ΔVCE/ro = 8/40 kΩ = 0.2 mA (a 10 % increase).

E6. Why must the base of a BJT be thin and lightly doped while the emitter is thick and heavily doped?

Thin base: injected electrons cross before recombining ⇒ base transport factor B → 1 and small base current. Light base doping: few holes to recombine with ⇒ smaller IB,rec, and fewer holes to be injected back into the emitter. Heavy emitter doping: the electron injection current from the emitter far exceeds the hole current back into it ⇒ γE → 1. Together α → 1 and β is large.

F. MOS and MOSFET

F1. Find Cox for tox = 5 nm SiO2. What happens to Cox and the field if tox is halved at the same VG?

Cox = 3.45×10-13/5×10-7 = 6.9×10-7 F/cm² (0.69 μF/cm²). Halving tox doubles Cox and doubles the oxide field V/tox. Higher Cox ⇒ more inversion charge and more current for the same overdrive; the price is oxide reliability and tunnelling leakage.

F2. For an n-type MOS capacitor (n-substrate), name the state at (a) large positive VG, (b) small negative VG, (c) large negative VG.

(a) Accumulation (electrons attracted to the interface). (b) Depletion (electrons repelled, uncovered donor ions +). (c) Inversion (holes collect at the surface, forming a p-type channel: the pMOS channel).

F3. nMOS: μnCox = 200 μA/V², W/L = 5, Vth = 0.5 V. Find ID at VGS = 1.5 V for VDS = 0.4 V, 0.8 V, 3 V. Also gm in saturation.

k′W/L = 1 mA/V²; Vov = 1.0 V. VDS = 0.4: triode: 1 × (1×0.4 − 0.08) = 0.32 mA. VDS = 0.8: triode: 1 × (0.8 − 0.32) = 0.48 mA. VDS = 3: saturation (3 ≥ 1): ½ × 1 × 1² = 0.5 mA. gm = k′(W/L)Vov = 1 mS. Notice the current rises quickly then flattens at 0.5 mA, the peak of the triode parabola at VDS = Vov.

F4. Derive, in five lines, the triode current of an nMOS.
  1. Q(x) = W Cox(VGS − Vth − V(x)).
  2. v = μ𝓔 = μ dV/dx (magnitude).
  3. I = Q v = W Cox(VGS − Vth − V) μ dV/dx.
  4. Integrate ∫0L I dx = μ W Cox ∫0VDS (VGS − Vth − V) dV.
  5. I L = μ W Cox[(VGS − Vth)VDS − VDS²/2] ⇒ ID = μnCox(W/L)[…].
F5. Why do pMOS transistors in a CMOS inverter have W about 2 to 3 times larger than the nMOS?

Holes have a lower mobility (μp ≈ μn/2 to /3) so for equal W/L the pMOS conducts less current and charges the load slower. Making Wp ≈ 2 to 3 × Wn equalises the drive currents and gives equal rise and fall times.

F6. An nMOS switch (RON = 1 kΩ) drives a 20 fF load. What is τ? What limits how small you can make τ?

τ = RC = 1 kΩ × 20 fF = 20 ps. Increasing W lowers RON but also raises the transistor's own parasitic capacitance and the load presented to the previous stage. Velocity saturation and interconnect resistance also set limits.

H. The MOSFET in depth (Chapter 11)

H1. nMOS with μnCox(W/L) = 2 mA/V², Vth = 0.6 V, VGS = 1.4 V. Find the region and ID for VDS = 0.3 V and 1.5 V.

Vov = 0.8 V. VDS = 0.3 < 0.8 ⇒ triode: 2 × (0.8 × 0.3 − 0.045) = 0.39 mA. VDS = 1.5 ≥ 0.8 ⇒ saturation: ½ × 2 × 0.64 = 0.64 mA.

H2. pMOS: μpCox = 60 μA/V², W/L = 20, Vtp = −0.5 V. Source at 1.8 V, gate at 0.6 V, drain at 0.9 V. Region and current?

Use magnitudes: |VGS| = 1.2 V, overdrive 1.2 − 0.5 = 0.7 V, |VDS| = 0.9 V ≥ 0.7 ⇒ saturation. kp = 60 × 20 = 1.2 mA/V². ISD = ½ × 1.2 × 0.49 = 0.294 mA, flowing from source to drain.

H3. An nMOS (k = 0.4 mA/V², Vth = 0.5 V, VGS = 1.5 V) has RD from VDD = 3 V to the drain. Find ID and VDS for RD = 5 kΩ and 20 kΩ.

5 kΩ: assume saturation: ID = ½ × 0.4 × 1² = 0.2 mA; VDS = 3 − 0.2 × 5 = 2 V ≥ 1 V ✓. ID = 0.2 mA, VDS = 2 V.

20 kΩ: saturation would give VDS = 3 − 4 = −1 V: impossible, so the device is in triode. Solve 0.4(VDS − VDS²/2) = (3 − VDS)/20 ⇒ 4VDS² − 9VDS + 3 = 0 ⇒ VDS = (9 − √33)/8 = 0.41 V, ID = (3 − 0.41)/20 = 0.13 mA. Check 0.41 < 1 ✓.

H4. A process has n = 1.5. Find the sub-threshold slope. With Vth = 0.45 V, by how many decades does the current drop from VGS = Vth to VGS = 0?

S = 1.5 × 0.0259 × ln10 = 89 mV/decade. 450/89 = 5 decades (a factor of 105).

H5. In saturation an nMOS carries 1.0 mA at VDS = 1 V and 1.1 mA at VDS = 3 V. Find λ, VA and ro.

1.1/1.0 = (1 + 3λ)/(1 + λ) ⇒ 1.1 + 1.1λ = 1 + 3λ ⇒ λ = 0.053 V-1, VA = 19 V. ro = ΔV/ΔI = 2 V/0.1 mA = 20 kΩ.

H6. Vth0 = 0.4 V, γ = 0.5 V½, 2φF = 0.8 V. What VSB raises Vth to 0.6 V?

0.2 = 0.5(√(0.8 + VSB) − 0.894) ⇒ √(0.8 + VSB) = 1.294 ⇒ VSB = 0.88 V.

H7. A process is scaled by S = 1.4 (one "node") with constant-field scaling. What happens to area, delay, power per gate and power density? What if voltage is held constant instead?

Constant field: area × 1/1.96 = 0.51, delay × 0.71, power × 0.51, power density × 1. Constant voltage: delay × 1/1.96 = 0.51, power × 1.4, power density × 1.4³ = 2.7, fields × 1.4.

H8. With Ec = 4 V/μm, compare the velocity-saturation factor 1/(1 + VDS/EcL) at VDS = 1 V for L = 2 μm and L = 50 nm. Why does the short device's current become linear in Vov?

L = 2 μm: EcL = 8 V ⇒ factor 1/1.125 = 0.89. L = 50 nm: EcL = 0.2 V ⇒ 1/6 = 0.17. Carriers move at vsat regardless of the field, so I = (charge per length) × vsat = WCoxVovvsat: linear in Vov.

I. CMOS inverter and gates (Chapter 12)

I1. VDD = 3.3 V, Vtn = |Vtp| = 0.5 V. Find VM when kn = kp and when kn = 4kp.

kn = kp: VM = 1.65 V (= VDD/2). kn = 4kp: r = 0.5 ⇒ VM = (0.5 + 0.5 × 2.8)/1.5 = 1.27 V; the stronger nMOS pulls the threshold down.

I2. Matched inverter, VDD = 3.3 V, Vt = 0.6 V. Find VIL, VIH, NML, NMH.

VIL = (9.9 + 1.2)/8 = 1.39 V; VIH = (16.5 − 1.2)/8 = 1.91 V; NML = 1.39 − 0 = 1.39 V; NMH = 3.3 − 1.91 = 1.39 V.

I3. Rn = 8 kΩ, Rp = 20 kΩ, CL = 15 fF. Find tpHL, tpLH, tp, and the pMOS width factor that balances them.

tpHL = 0.69 × 8k × 15f = 83 ps; tpLH = 0.69 × 20k × 15f = 207 ps; tp = 145 ps. Widen the pMOS by 20/8 = 2.5×.

I4. A chip has 107 gates, each driving 2 fF, VDD = 1 V, clock 2 GHz, activity 0.1. Dynamic power?

P = 0.1 × 107 × 2×10-15 × 1² × 2×109 = 4 W.

I5. Design static CMOS gates for (a) Y = ((A + B)C)′ and (b) Y = (AB + C)′.

(a) PDN: (A ∥ B) in series with C. PUN: (A series B) in parallel with C. 6 transistors.

(b) PDN: (A series B) in parallel with C. PUN: (A ∥ B) in series with C. 6 transistors.

I6. How many transistors for a 4-input NOR in static CMOS and in pseudo-nMOS? Give one advantage and two disadvantages of pseudo-nMOS.

Static CMOS 8; pseudo-nMOS 5. Advantage: fewer transistors and less input capacitance (and no slow 4-high pMOS stack). Disadvantages: static current whenever the output is low; VOL > 0 (ratioed), so smaller noise margin.

I7. Your notebook photo: Av = 100. What output change does a 2 mV input change cause at the switching point? Why is high gain good for logic?

|ΔVout| = 100 × 2 mV = 0.2 V (in the opposite direction). High gain means a narrow transition region, so wide noise margins and quick restoration of degraded levels.

I8. List the static properties of the CMOS inverter and explain each in one line.

(1) Zero static power: one transistor is always off. (2) High input impedance: the input is an insulated gate. (3) Low output impedance: the output is always tied to a rail through an ON device. (4) Full swing, ratioless: VOH = VDD, VOL = 0 regardless of sizing.

J. Unit I and MOS extras (Chapter 13)

J1. Estimate ni of Si at 400 K (Nc, Nv ∝ T3/2, Eg = 1.12 eV).

√(NcNv) at 400 K = 1.71×1019 × (4/3)1.5 = 2.63×1019. kT = 0.0345 eV; Eg/2kT = 16.25 ⇒ e−16.25 = 8.8×10-8. ni ≈ 2.3×1012 cm-3, about 300 times its 300 K value.

J2. Si doped with P (Ec − ED = 45 meV) at ND = 1016, 300 K. What fraction of donors is ionised?

Ec − EF ≈ 0.206 eV, so EF − ED = 0.045 − 0.206 = −0.161 eV. Fraction = 1/(1 + 2e−0.161/0.0259) = 1/(1 + 0.004) = 99.6 %: full ionisation is a good assumption.

J3. Cut-off wavelength of Ge (0.66 eV). Can a Si photodiode detect 1.55 μm light?

Ge: 1.24/0.66 = 1.88 μm. Si cuts off at 1.1 μm, so no: 1.55 μm photons (0.8 eV) are below its gap. That is why Ge or InGaAs detectors are used for fibre-optic light.

J4. After the light is switched off, Δn falls to 10 % of its value in 4.6 μs. Find τ.

e−t/τ = 0.1 ⇒ t = τ ln 10 ⇒ τ = 4.6/2.303 = 2 μs.

J5. A p⁺n diode's 1/C² (per area²) vs V plot has slope −1.2×1015 cm⁴F-2V-1 and meets the V axis at 0.8 V. Find ND and Vbi.

ND = 2/(qεs|slope|) = 2/(1.6×10-19 × 1.04×10-12 × 1.2×1015) = 1.0×1016 cm-3; Vbi = 0.8 V.

J6. The forward current of a diode rises ×10 for every 120 mV. Find η and the dominant current mechanism.

Ideal is 59.6 mV/decade (η = 1). 120/59.6 = η ≈ 2 ⇒ recombination current in the depletion region dominates (typical at low forward bias).

J7. Repeat the BJT example of §13.16 with the base width halved (W = 0.5 μm). What happens to β?

B = 1/cosh(0.05) = 0.99875; γ = 1 − 0.0005 = 0.9995 (W also enters γ). α ≈ 0.99825 ⇒ β ≈ 570 (vs 166). A thinner base sharply raises β, at the cost of a lower Early voltage and easier punch-through.

J8. A red LED emits at 620 nm. Estimate its band gap and turn-on voltage.

Eg = 1242/620 = 2.0 eV; turn-on ≈ 1.8 to 2.0 V (close to Eg/q, slightly below).

J9. For NA = 1017 cm-3, find φF and the band bending at the onset of strong inversion. Describe the surface at that point.

φF = 0.0259 ln(1017/1.5×1010) = 0.407 V; ψs = 2φF = 0.81 V. The surface electron density equals the bulk hole density (1017): the surface is as n-type as the bulk is p-type.

J10. Explain why a GaN diode leaks far less in reverse than a Si diode, and why a GaN power device can block more voltage in the same thickness.

Reverse current ∝ ni² (diffusion) and ∝ ni (generation); ni ∝ e−Eg/2kT is astronomically smaller for 3.4 eV than for 1.1 eV. Blocking: VBR = ½WFcrit, and Fcrit is ~3 MV/cm for GaN vs 0.4 MV/cm for Si, so ~7× more voltage for the same W.

K. Manufacturing (Chapter 14)

K1. A plane cuts the axes at x = 2, y = 3 and is parallel to z. Miller indices?

(2, 3, ∞) → (½, ⅓, 0) → ×6 → (3 2 0).

K2. With A = 0.165 μm and B = 0.0117 μm²/h, how long does a 0.2 μm oxide take? How much silicon is consumed?

t = (x² + Ax)/B = (0.04 + 0.033)/0.0117 = 6.2 h. Si consumed = 0.44 × 0.2 = 88 nm.

K3. Give the reactions for dry and wet oxidation and say which is used for the gate oxide and why.

Dry: Si + O2 → SiO2. Wet: Si + 2H2O → SiO2 + 2H2. Dry for the gate: slower but denser, fewer defects and traps, better breakdown. Wet is for thick field oxides where speed matters.

K4. A boron implant: dose 5×1014 cm-2, ΔRp = 0.05 μm. Peak concentration? Why must it be annealed?

Cp = 5×1014/(2.507 × 5×10-6) = 4.0×1019 cm-3. Annealing repairs the lattice damage from nuclear stopping and moves the B atoms onto substitutional sites where they are electrically active.

K5. (a) Resolution of 248 nm lithography with NA = 0.8, k1 = 0.35. (b) What NA is needed for 50 nm features at 193 nm with k1 = 0.3? Is that possible in air?

(a) R = 0.35 × 248/0.8 = 109 nm. (b) NA = 0.3 × 193/50 = 1.16 > 1, impossible in air (n = 1); it needs immersion (water, n = 1.44).

K6. Pre-deposition vs drive-in: boundary condition, profile, and what happens to the surface concentration and dose in each.

Pre-dep: constant surface concentration Cs (unlimited source), erfc profile, dose grows as √t. Drive-in: fixed dose (source removed), Gaussian profile, surface concentration falls as 1/√t while the junction deepens.

K7. In the NMOS process, what do HF and piranha do, and how many masks are used?

HF etches SiO2 through the resist openings; piranha (H2SO4 + H2O2) strips the photoresist. Four masks: S/D windows, gate region, contact openings, metal pattern.

K8. In CZ growth, what sets the ingot diameter, why are the crucible and seed counter-rotated, and what are the two main contaminants?

The pull rate (and melt temperature) sets the diameter. Counter-rotation stirs the melt for a uniform temperature (no hot/cold spots) and uniform doping. Contaminants: oxygen from the quartz crucible and carbon from the graphite parts.

K9. CVD vs PVD: one difference in mechanism and one in step coverage. Name three epitaxy methods.

CVD: gases react chemically on the surface; conformal, good step coverage. PVD: a solid is vaporised (evaporation, sputtering) and condenses; line-of-sight, shadowing. Epitaxy: VPE, LPE, MBE.

L. SPICE and LTspice (Chapter 15)

L1. Write a netlist for a CMOS inverter (nMOS NMOS180 W = 1 μm, pMOS PMOS180 W = 2.5 μm, L = 0.18 μm, VDD = 1.8 V) and a DC sweep of its VTC.

VDD vdd 0 1.8
VIN in 0 0
MP out in vdd vdd PMOS180 W=2.5u L=0.18u
MN out in 0 0 NMOS180 W=1u L=0.18u
.include models180.lib
.dc VIN 0 1.8 0.01

L2. A diode model has Is = 100 pA and n = 1.679. Find its current at 0.6 V.

I = 10-10 × e0.6/(1.679 × 0.0259) = 10-10 × e13.8 ≈ 98 μA (close to the "1 mA diode" name only near 0.7 V).

L3. Which MOSFET model would you use for (a) hand calculation, (b) a 45 nm sign-off simulation, (c) a low-power analog circuit in weak inversion? Why?

(a) Level 1 (square law, few parameters). (b) BSIM (captures short-channel effects; > 100 parameters). (c) EKV (one continuous expression from weak to strong inversion), or BSIM.

L4. Name the four main SPICE analyses and what each is for.

DC (operating point, sweeps, transfer curves), AC (small-signal frequency response), transient (time waveforms), Monte Carlo (statistical variation of components).

M. Semiconductor memories (Chapter 16)

M1. A 4 Mbit square array: rows, columns, row and column address bits.

222 bits = 211 × 211 ⇒ 2048 × 2048; 11 + 11 address bits.

M2. In the board's 4×4 NOR ROM, what word is read when R2 is selected? Where would you add a transistor to make R2 read 0001?

R2 has transistors at C1 and C2 ⇒ 0011. For 0001 add a transistor at (R2, C3).

M3. A DRAM bit line is 300 fF, VDD = 1.2 V, precharge 0.6 V. What cell capacitance gives a 100 mV read signal?

0.6 × CS/(CS + 300) = 0.1 ⇒ 0.5CS = 30 ⇒ CS = 60 fF.

M4. Compare SRAM and DRAM on cell size, refresh, speed and use. Why is the DRAM read destructive?

SRAM: 6T, no refresh, fastest, caches. DRAM: 1T1C, needs refresh, slower, densest, main memory. Reading connects CS to the bit line and its charge is shared away, so the sense amplifier must rewrite it.

M5. Classify: mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash, SRAM, DRAM as volatile or non-volatile, and give the one-line difference between EPROM and EEPROM.

Non-volatile: mask ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash. Volatile: SRAM, DRAM. EPROM is erased with UV light (whole chip); EEPROM is erased electrically (byte by byte).

N. Explain-in-words questions (viva / short-answer)

N1. Why is the Fermi level called an "imaginary construct"?

Because it is just the energy at which f(E) = ½. There need not be any allowed state at that energy; in a semiconductor EF usually sits inside the forbidden gap.

N2. Why is there no net current at thermal equilibrium even though carriers keep diffusing and drifting?

At every point the diffusion current is exactly cancelled by an equal and opposite drift current (in the junction: Idiffusion = Idrift = Is). This is equivalent to EF being flat throughout the device.

N3. What two things must be true for a hole to be a useful concept?

The valence band must be nearly full (so tracking the few empty states is simpler), and the empty state must respond to fields like a particle with positive charge and positive effective mass. Both hold in a semiconductor.

N4. Why does the depletion region penetrate more into the lightly doped side?

The uncovered charge on both sides must be equal: q ND xn = q NA xp. Fewer ions per unit volume on the light side, so a larger thickness is needed to hold the same total charge.

N5. Why does a MOSFET need almost no gate current?

The gate is separated from the channel by an insulating oxide, forming a capacitor. Only charging current flows while the gate voltage changes; in DC the oxide blocks current. Field effect: the field, not a current, controls the channel.

N6. Compare BJT and MOSFET in one table.
BJTMOSFET
Controlbase current (current-controlled)gate voltage (voltage-controlled)
Input currentIB ≠ 0≈ 0 (insulated gate)
Carriersboth electrons and holes (bipolar)one type (unipolar)
I–V lawexponential IC ∝ eVBE/VTsquare law ID ∝ (VGS − Vth)²
Static power in logichigh≈ 0 in CMOS
Packing densitylowvery high ⇒ VLSI
Best athigh-speed analog, high gm per areadigital logic, memory, low power
N7. Why is the pull-up made of pMOS and the pull-down of nMOS, and not the other way round?

An nMOS turns off when its source rises to VDD − Vtn, so it can only pass a weak 1; a pMOS can only pass a weak 0. Putting pMOS to VDD and nMOS to GND lets each pass the level it passes strongly, giving full-swing outputs.

N8. Why was constant-voltage scaling preferred, and what problem does it create?

Supply voltages are standards shared by many chips, so they could not drop every generation. Keeping V fixed while shrinking dimensions raises the electric fields (×S) and power density (×S³): velocity saturation, hot carriers, DIBL, oxide breakdown and heat.

N9. Why does the oxide grow at the Si/SiO2 interface, and why does growth slow down?

The oxidant must diffuse through the oxide to reach silicon, where it reacts. As the oxide thickens the diffusion path lengthens, so the flux falls: growth changes from linear (reaction-limited) to parabolic (diffusion-limited).

N10. Why does ion implantation need an anneal but diffusion does not?

Implanted ions arrive with high energy, knock Si atoms out of place (crystal damage) and mostly stop in interstitial sites, where they are inactive. Annealing repairs the lattice and makes them substitutional. Diffusion happens slowly at high temperature, near equilibrium, so atoms already sit on lattice sites.

N11. Why must DRAM be refreshed but SRAM need not be?

DRAM stores the bit as charge on a tiny capacitor that leaks away through the junction and the off transistor in milliseconds. SRAM stores it in a feedback loop of two inverters, which actively restores the levels as long as power is on.

N12. Name three reasons silicon dominates over Ge and GaAs for VLSI.

(1) It grows an excellent native oxide (SiO2) with a near-perfect interface. (2) Its 1.1 eV gap keeps leakage low at operating temperature (Ge leaks). (3) Abundant, cheap, mechanically strong, available as huge defect-free CZ wafers.

CHAPTER 19Cram Sheet: Traps, Comparisons and Corrections

19.1 The 30 things most likely to lose marks

  1. Band gaps: Ge 0.7, Si 1.1, GaAs 1.34, GaN 3.4 eV. Si and Ge are indirect; GaAs and GaN are direct.
  2. kBT = 25.87 meV at 300 K, VT = 25.9 mV. Use eV vs J consistently.
  3. At T = 0 K: f = 1 below EF, ½ at EF, 0 above.
  4. m* ∝ 1/curvature; more curvature = lighter = more mobile = more current.
  5. μn > μp because mh* > me*.
  6. Mobility vs T is a hill: impurity scattering at low T, phonons at high T; Matthiessen's rule adds reciprocals.
  7. Diffusion: Jn = +qDndn/dx, Jp = −qDpdp/dx. Einstein: D = μVT.
  8. np = ni² only at equilibrium; U = 0 there.
  9. Depletion region: xn/xp = NA/ND; more into the lighter side. Bias enters as (V0 ± V).
  10. Flat EF = no current; sloped bands = field.
  11. Is has D/(L N) with the opposite side's doping; smaller ni (larger Eg) ⇒ smaller Is ⇒ larger forward voltage (Si > Ge).
  12. Zener < 5 V (tunnelling, heavy doping); avalanche > 8 V (impact ionisation, light doping).
  13. BJT: active = F/R; α = Bγ; β = α/(1−α); thin light base, heavy emitter; Early voltage from base-width modulation.
  14. MOS capacitor (p-substrate): negative VG accumulation, small + depletion, large + inversion. 1/C = 1/Cox + 1/Cdep; Cmin at w = wm.
  15. MOSFET triode current has W/L and the VDS²/2 term; saturation begins at VDS = VGS − Vth.
  16. Saturation starts at VDS = VGS − Vth; ID,sat = ½k(Vov)². Assume saturation, then check.
  17. Body effect: VSB ↑ ⇒ Vth ↑. DIBL: VDS ↑ ⇒ Vth ↓. CLM: ID(1 + λVDS), VA = 1/λ.
  18. Sub-threshold slope ≥ 60 mV/decade at 300 K. Velocity saturation makes ID linear in Vov.
  19. Constant-field scaling keeps power density constant; constant-voltage scaling raises it by S³.
  20. CMOS inverter: pMOS pull-up, nMOS pull-down; zero static power, high Zin, low Zout, full swing.
  21. VM where Vout = Vin, both transistors saturated; VDD/2 needs (W/L)p ≈ 2 to 3 (W/L)n.
  22. Noise margins from the slope = −1 points: NML = VIL − VOL, NMH = VOH − VIH. Delay 0.69RC. P = αCVDD²f.
  23. PDN: AND series, OR parallel; PUN is the dual; output inverted.
  24. Ionisation: donor factor 2, acceptor factor 4. Boltzmann needs 3kT clearance. λc = 1.24/Eg μm.
  25. Recombination current η = 2 (forward, low V); generation current ∝ W (reverse creeps up).
  26. Zener ≈ < 4Eg/q (heavy doping), avalanche > 6Eg/q (light doping); VBR = ½WFcrit.
  27. 1/C² vs V: slope ⇒ ND, intercept ⇒ Vbi. HF C–V stays at Cmin; LF returns to Cox; deep depletion goes below.
  28. Oxide: 44 % consumed Si; thin linear, thick parabolic. Pre-dep erfc (fixed Cs), drive-in Gaussian (fixed Q). Light ions go deeper; implants need annealing.
  29. Positive resist: pattern = mask. R = k1λ/NA. CZ: pull rate sets diameter; O and C contamination.
  30. Memory: word lines = rows, bit lines = columns; capacity 2N×2M; NOR ROM transistor = 0; DRAM 1T1C refresh, SRAM 6T no refresh.

19.4 Seven-day plan to top the test

  1. Day 1: Chapters 0 to 3, plus §13.1 to 13.2. Redo the f(E), E–k and DOS questions. Draw the band pictures from memory.
  2. Day 2: Chapters 4 to 6, plus §13.3 to 13.8. Practice B, C and J1 to J4 without looking.
  3. Day 3: Chapter 7, plus §13.9 to 13.14. Derive I = Is(eV/VT − 1) and Vbi out loud. Practice D and J5 to J10.
  4. Day 4: Chapters 8 and 9, plus §13.15 to 13.16. Draw the C–V curves (LF, HF, deep depletion). Practice E and F1, F2.
  5. Day 5: Chapters 10 and 11. Fill in the regions table from memory; solve every worked example. Practice F3 to F6 and H.
  6. Day 6: Chapters 12, 15 and 16. Design NAND, NOR, (AB + CD)′ and the NOR ROM on paper. Practice I, L and M.
  7. Day 7: Chapter 14, then the formula sheet (Chapter 17) and §19.1 to 19.3. Practice K, then N1 to N12 timed as a viva.
Final pep talk, like I'm 10

Every device in this course is just one idea repeated: carriers are pushed (drift) or spread (diffusion), and something blocks or opens their path. In the diode the blocker is the depletion region; in the BJT it is a thin base; in the MOSFET it is a gate-controlled channel; in CMOS logic it is one of two doors that is always shut; and in the factory every step just decides where those carriers and barriers end up. If you can draw the band picture and say who is pushing whom, you can answer nearly any question.
